          <h1>
            ArrayToString<br>
            <small>Calling toString on an array does not provide useful information</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">toString</code> method on an array will print its identity, such as
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[I@4488aabb</code>. This is almost never needed. Use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Arrays.toString</code> to print a
human-readable summary.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ArrayToString")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ArraysAsListPrimitiveArray<br>
            <small>Arrays.asList does not autobox primitive arrays, as one might expect.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Arrays.asList does not autobox primitive arrays, as one might expect. If you
intended to autobox the primitive array, use an asList method from Guava that
does autobox. If you intended to create a singleton list containing the
primitive array, use Collections.singletonList to make your intent clearer.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ArraysAsListPrimitiveArray")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            AsyncCallableReturnsNull<br>
            <small>AsyncCallable should not return a null Future, only a Future whose result is null.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Methods like Futures.whenAllComplete(…).callAsync(…) will throw a
NullPointerException if the provided AsyncCallable returns a null Future. To
produce a Future with an output of null, instead return immediateFuture(null).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AsyncCallableReturnsNull")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            AutoValueConstructorOrderChecker<br>
            <small>Arguments to AutoValue constructor are in the wrong order</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>AutoValue constructors are synthesized with their parameters in the same order
as the abstract accessor methods. Calls to the constructor need to match this
ordering.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AutoValueConstructorOrderChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            BadAnnotationImplementation<br>
            <small>Classes that implement Annotation must override equals and hashCode. Consider using AutoAnnotation instead of implementing Annotation by hand.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Implementations of <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/annotation/Annotation.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Annotation</code></a> must override <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> to match
the expectations defined in that interface, to ensure compatibility with the
annotation instances that source annotations create. Without this, operations
that care about equality of annotations (such as qualified dependency injection
bindings) will fail in mysterious ways.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@SomeAnnotation</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">annotatedMethod</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>

  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">HelloAnnotationImpl</span> <span class="kd">implements</span> <span class="nc">SomeAnnotation</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@Override</span>
    <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">Class</span><span class="o">&lt;?</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">Annotation</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">annotationType</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">SomeAnnotation</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>

    <span class="nd">@Override</span>
    <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="nf">value</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Annotation</span> <span class="n">manual</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">HelloAnnotationImpl</span><span class="o">();</span>
    <span class="nc">Annotation</span> <span class="n">fromMethod</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMethod</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"annotatedMethod"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">getDeclaredAnnotations</span><span class="o">()[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">];</span>

    <span class="n">manual</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">fromMethod</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// false, violating equality expectations of Annotation!</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>It is very difficult to write these methods correctly, so consider using
<a href="https://github.com/google/auto/blob/master/value/src/main/java/com/google/auto/value/AutoAnnotation.java"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoAnnotation</code></a> to generate a properly-functioning implementation of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Annotation</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@SomeAnnotation</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">annotatedMethod</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>

  <span class="nd">@AutoAnnotation</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">SomeAnnotation</span> <span class="nf">someAnnotationInstance</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">value</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">AutoAnnotation_Foo_someAnnotationInstance</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">value</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Annotation</span> <span class="n">manual</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">someAnnotationInstance</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="nc">Annotation</span> <span class="n">fromMethod</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMethod</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"annotatedMethod"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">getDeclaredAnnotations</span><span class="o">()[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">];</span>

    <span class="n">manual</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">fromMethod</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// true, hooray!</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BadAnnotationImplementation")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            BadShiftAmount<br>
            <small>Shift by an amount that is out of range</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>For shift operations on int types, only the five lowest-order bits of the shift
amount are used as the shift distance. This means that shift amounts that are
not in the range 0 to 31, inclusive, are silently mapped to values in that
range. For example, a shift of an int by 32 is equivalent to shifting by 0,
i.e., a no-op.</p>

<p>See JLS 15.19, “Shift Operators”, for more details.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BadShiftAmount")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            BanJNDI<br>
            <small>Using JNDI may deserialize user input via the `Serializable` API which is extremely dangerous</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>JNDI (“Java Naming and Directory Interface”) is a Java JDK API representing an
abstract directory service such as DNS, a file system or LDAP. Critically, JNDI
allows Java objects to be serialized and deserialized on the wire in
implementing systems. This means that if a Java application is allowed to
perform a JNDI lookup over some transport protocol then the server it connects
to can execute arbitrary attacker-defined code. See
<a href="https://www.blackhat.com/docs/us-16/materials/us-16-Munoz-A-Journey-From-JNDI-LDAP-Manipulation-To-RCE.pdf">this</a>
Black Hat talk for more information.</p>

<p>This checker bans usage of every API in the Java JDK that can result in
deserialising an unsafe object via JNDI. The list of APIs is generated from
static callgraph analysis of the JDK, rooted at <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.Context.lookup</code>
and is as follows:</p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.Context.lookup</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.jdo.JDOHelper.getPersistenceManagerFactory</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.jdo.JDOHelperTest.testGetPMFBadJNDI</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.jdo.JDOHelperTest.testGetPMFBadJNDIGoodClassLoader</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.jdo.JDOHelperTest.testGetPMFNullJNDI</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.jdo.JDOHelperTest.testGetPMFNullJNDIGoodClassLoader</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.management.remote.JMXConnectorFactory.connect</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.management.remote.rmi.RMIConnector.connect</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.management.remote.rmi.RMIConnector.findRMIServer</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.management.remote.rmi.RMIConnector.findRMIServerJNDI</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.management.remote.rmi.RMIConnector.RMIClientCommunicatorAdmin.doStart</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.directory.InitialDirContext.bind</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.directory.InitialDirContext.createSubcontext</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.directory.InitialDirContext.getAttributes</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.directory.InitialDirContext.getSchema</code></li>

  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.spi.ContinuationContext.lookup</code></li>

  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.spi.ContinuationDirContext.getSchemaClassDefinition</code></li>

  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.spi.ContinuationDirContext.search</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.sql.rowset.spi.ProviderImpl.getDataSourceLock</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.sql.rowset.spi.ProviderImpl.getProviderGrade</code></li>

<p>A small subset of these are banned directly. The rest are banned indirectly by
banning the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">lookup()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">bind()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">rebind()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getAttributes()</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">modifyAttriutes()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">createSubcontext()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getSchema()</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getSchemaClassDefinition()</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">search()</code> methods on any subclass
(implementer) of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.naming.Context</code>. The indirect ban is necessary due to
these methods being vulnerable in previously noted subclasses in the JDK. If
they were not banned at the Context level, a cast to Context would make the
vulnerable call invisible to static analysis.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BanJNDI")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            BoxedPrimitiveEquality<br>
            <small>Comparison using reference equality instead of value equality. Reference equality of boxed primitive types is usually not useful, as they are value objects, and it is bug-prone, as instances are cached for some values but not others.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: NumericEquality</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Comparison using reference equality instead of value equality. The inputs to
this comparison are boxed primitive types, where reference equality is
particularly bug-prone: Primitive wrapper classes cache instances for some (but
usually not all) values, so == may be equivalent to equals() for some values but
not others. Additionally, not all versions of the runtime and other libraries
use the cache in the same cases, so upgrades may change behavior. Furthermore,
reference identity is usually not useful for primitive wrappers, as they are
immutable types whose equals() method fully compares their values.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BoxedPrimitiveEquality")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ChainingConstructorIgnoresParameter<br>
            <small>The called constructor accepts a parameter with the same name and type as one of its caller's parameters, but its caller doesn't pass that parameter to it.  It's likely that it was intended to.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When a class exposes multiple constructors, they’re generally used as a means of
initializing default parameters. If a chaining constructor ignores a parameter,
it’s likely the parameter needed to be plumbed to the chained constructor.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">MissileLauncher</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Location</span> <span class="n">target</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">target</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
<span class="nc">MissileLauncher</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">askForConfirmation</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="no">TEST_TARGET</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// should be askForConfirmation</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
<span class="nc">MissileLauncher</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Location</span> <span class="n">target</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">askForConfirmation</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
   <span class="o">...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ChainingConstructorIgnoresParameter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

            CheckNotNullMultipleTimes<br>
            <small>A variable was checkNotNulled multiple times. Did you mean to check something else?</small>

<html>

  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="chrome=1">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>CheckReturnValue</title>
  <link href="/stylesheets/bootstrap.min.css" rel="stylesheet">
  <link href="/stylesheets/styles.css" rel="stylesheet">

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            CheckReturnValue<br>
            <small>The result of this call must be used</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: ResultOfMethodCallIgnored, ReturnValueIgnored</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When code calls a non-<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void</code> method, it should usually use the value that the
method returns.</p>

<p>Consider the following code, which ignores the return value of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">concat</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">string</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">concat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"\n"</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>That code is a no-op because <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">concat</code> doesn’t modify <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">string</code>; it returns a new
string for the caller to use, as in:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">string</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">string</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">concat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"\n"</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To avoid this bug, Error Prone requires callers to use the return value of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">concat</code> and some other well-known methods.</p>

<p>Additionally, Error Prone can be configured to require callers to use the return
value of any methods that you choose.</p>

<h3 id="how-to-tell-error-prone-which-methods-to-check">How to tell Error Prone which methods to check</h3>

<p>Most methods are like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">concat</code>: Calls to those methods must use their return
values.</p>

<p>However, there are exceptions. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">set.add(element)</code> returns a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">boolean</code>: The return value is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">false</code> if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">element</code> was <em>already</em> contained in
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">set</code>. Typically, callers don’t need to know this, so they don’t need to use the
return value.</p>

<p>For Error Prone’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">CheckReturnValue</code> check to be useful, it needs to know which
methods are like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">concat</code> and which are like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">add</code>.</p>

<h4 id="checkreturnvalue-and-canignorereturnvalue"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CanIgnoreReturnValue</code></h4>

<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code> annotation (available in JSR-305<sup id="fnref:jsr" role="doc-noteref"><a href="#fn:jsr" class="footnote" rel="footnote">1</a></sup> or in
<a href="https://errorprone.info/api/latest/com/google/errorprone/annotations/CheckReturnValue.html">Error Prone</a>) marks methods whose return values must be used. This error
is triggered when one of these methods is called but the result is not used.</p>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code> may be applied to a class or package <sup id="fnref:package-info" role="doc-noteref"><a href="#fn:package-info" class="footnote" rel="footnote">2</a></sup> to
indicate that all methods in that class or package must have their return values
used.</p>

<p>For convenience, we provide an annotation, <a href="https://errorprone.info/api/latest/com/google/errorprone/annotations/CanIgnoreReturnValue.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CanIgnoreReturnValue</code></a>, to
exempt specific methods or classes from this behavior. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CanIgnoreReturnValue</code>
is available from the Error Prone annotations package,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations</code>.</p>

<p>If you really want to ignore the return value of a method annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code>, a cleaner alternative to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings</code> is to assign
the result to a variable that starts with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">unused</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">setNameFormat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">nameFormat</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">unused</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">format</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">nameFormat</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// fail fast if the format is bad or null</span>
  <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">nameFormat</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">nameFormat</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h3 id="ignored-contexts">Ignored contexts</h3>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code> is ignored under the following conditions (which saves users
from having to use either an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">unused</code> variable or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings</code>):</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p>Calls from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Mockito.verify()</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stubber.when()</code>; e.g.,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Mockito.verify(t).foo()</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doReturn(val).when(t).foo()</code> (where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">foo()</code> is
annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code>). Here, the method calls are just used to
program the mock object, not to be consumed directly.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>Code that does exception testing with JUnit, where the intent is that the
method call should throw an exception:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p>Uses of JUnit 4.13 or JUnit5’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertThrows</code> methods:</p>

        <div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">assertThrows</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">IndexOutOfBoundsException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">(-</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">));</span>
</code></pre></div>        </div>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">try/execute/fail/catch</code> pattern</p>

        <div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code> <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
   <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">(-</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
   <span class="n">fail</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Expected a IndexOutOfBoundsException to be thrown on a negative index"</span><span class="o">);</span>
 <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">IndexOutOfBoundsException</span> <span class="n">expected</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
 <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div>        </div>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p>JUnit’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ExpectedException</code></p>

        <div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">expectedException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">expect</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">IndexOutOfBoundsException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">(-</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// If this throws IOOBE, the test passes.</span>
</code></pre></div>        </div>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ol>

<div class="footnotes" role="doc-endnotes">
  <ol>
    <li id="fn:jsr" role="doc-endnote">
      <p>Of note, the JSR-305 project was <a href="https://jcp.org/en/jsr/detail?id=305">never fully approved</a>, so the
JSR-305 version of the annotation is not actually official and causes
issues with Java 9 and the <a href="https://blog.codefx.org/java/jsr-305-java-9/">Module System</a>. Prefer to use the
Error Prone version. <a href="#fnref:jsr" class="reversefootnote" role="doc-backlink">&#8617;</a></p>
    </li>
    <li id="fn:package-info" role="doc-endnote">
      <p>To annotate a package, create a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">package-info.java</code> file in the package directory, add a package statement,
and annotate the package statement. <a href="#fnref:package-info" class="reversefootnote" role="doc-backlink">&#8617;</a></p>
    </li>
  </ol>
</div>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            CollectionIncompatibleType<br>
            <small>Incompatible type as argument to Object-accepting Java collections method</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Querying a collection for an element it cannot possibly contain is almost
certainly a bug.</p>

<p>In a generic collection type, query methods such as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map.get(Object)</code> and
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection.remove(Object)</code> accept a parameter that identifies a potential
element to <em>look for</em> in that collection. This check reports cases where this
element <em>cannot</em> be present because its type and the collection’s generic
element type are “incompatible.” A typical example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Set</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Long</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">values</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">...</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">contains</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">42</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This code looks reasonable, but there’s a problem: The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code> contains <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Long</code>
instances, but the argument to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains</code> is an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer</code>. Because no instance
can be of type <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer</code> and of type <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Long</code> at the same time, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains</code>
check always fails. This is clearly not what the developer intended.</p>

<p>Why does the collection API permit this kind of mistake? Why not declare the
method as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains(E)</code>? After all, that is what the collections API does for
methods that <em>store</em> an element in the collection: They require that passed type
be strictly <em>assignable to</em> the collection’s element type. For example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">addIntegerOne</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Set</span><span class="o">&lt;?</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">numbers</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">numbers</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">42</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// won't compile</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The code above rightly won’t compile, because <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">numbers</code> <em>might</em> be a (for
example) <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set&lt;Long&gt;</code>, and adding an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer</code> value would corrupt it.</p>

<p>But this restriction is necessary only for methods that insert elements. Methods
that only query or remove elements cannot corrupt the collection:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">removeIntegerOne</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Set</span><span class="o">&lt;?</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">numbers</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">numbers</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">remove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">42</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// should compile (and does)</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>In this case, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer</code> <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">42</code> might be contained in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">numbers</code>, and should be
removed if it is, but if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">numbers</code> is a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set&lt;Long&gt;</code>, no harm is done.</p>

<p>We’d like to define <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains</code> in a way that rejects the bad call but permits
the good one. But Java’s type system is not powerful enough. Our solution is
static analysis.</p>

<p>The specific restriction we would like to express for the two types is not
assignability, but “compatibility”. Informally, we mean that it must at least be
<em>possible</em> for some instance to be of both types. Formally, we require that a
“casting conversion” exist between the types as defined by
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se7/html/jls-5.html#jls-5.5.1">JLS 5.5.1</a>.</p>

<p>The result is that the method can be defined as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains(Object)</code>, permitting
the “good” call above, but that Error Prone will give errors for incompatible
arguments, preventing the “bad.”</p>

<h3 id="footnote-would-requiring-e-have-been-better">Footnote: Would requiring <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E</code> have been better?</h3>

<p>We might say: Sure, a buggy <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">remove</code> call can’t corrupt a collection. And sure,
someone might want to pass an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> reference that happens to contain an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E</code>.
But isn’t that a low standard for an API? We don’t normally write code that way:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">throwIfUnchecked</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">throwable</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="c1">// no "need" to require Throwable</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">throwable</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">RuntimeException</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">RuntimeException</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">throwable</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">throwable</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Error</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Error</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">throwable</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Such code would invite bugs. To avoid that, we require a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Throwable</code>. Users who
have an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> reference that might be a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Throwable</code> can test <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceof</code> and
cast. So why not require the same thing in the collections API?</p>

<p>Of course, we can’t really change the API of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection</code>. But if we were
designing a similar API, what would we do – require <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E</code> or accept any <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>?</p>

<p>The burden of proof falls on accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>, since doing so permits buggy
code. And we’re not going to settle for “it occasionally saves users a cast.”</p>

<p><em>The main reason to accept <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> is to permit a fast, type-safe <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set.equals</code>
implementation.</em></p>

<p>(<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> is actually just one example of the general problem, which arises with
many uses of wildcards. Once you’ve read the following, consider the problem of
implementing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection.removeAll(Collection&lt;?&gt;)</code> without <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains(Object)</code>.
Then consider how the problem would exist even if the signature were
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">removeAll(Collection&lt;? extends E&gt;)</code>. The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">removeAll</code> problem is at least
“solvable” by changing the signature to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">removeAll(Collection&lt;E&gt;)</code>, but that
signature may reject useful calls.)</p>

<p>Here’s how: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> necessarily accepts a plain <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>. It can test whether
that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> is a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>, but it can’t know the element type it was originally
declared with. In short, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> has to operate on a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set&lt;?&gt;</code>.</p>

<p>If <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">contains</code> were to require an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> would be in trouble because it
doesn’t know what <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E</code> is. In particular, it wouldn’t be able to call
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">otherSet.contains(myElement)</code> for any of its elements.</p>

<p>It would have only two options: It could copy the entire other <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code> into a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set&lt;Object&gt;</code>, or it could perform an unchecked cast. Copying is wasteful, so in
practice, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> would need an unchecked cast. This is probably acceptable,
but we might feel strange for defining an API that can be implemented only by
performing unchecked casts.</p>

<p>Does a cleaner implementation (and occasional convenience to callers) outweigh
the bugs that accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> enables? That’s a tough question. The good news
is that this Error Prone check gives you some of the best of both worlds.</p>

<h3 id="footnote-collection-containing-an-incompatible-type">Footnote: Collection containing an incompatible type</h3>

<p>It is technically possible for a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set&lt;Integer&gt;</code> to contain a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code> element,
but only if an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">unchecked</code> warning was earlier ignored or improperly suppressed.
Such practice should never be treated as acceptable, so it makes no practical
difference to our arguments above.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CollectionIncompatibleType")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ComparableType<br>
            <small>Implementing 'Comparable<T>' where T is not the same as the implementing class is incorrect, since it violates the symmetry contract of compareTo.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The type argument of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparable</code> should always be the type of the current
class.</p>

<p>For example, do this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="kd">implements</span> <span class="nc">Comparable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">compareTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>not this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="kd">implements</span> <span class="nc">Comparable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Bar</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">compareTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Bar</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Implementing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparable</code> for a different type breaks the API contract, which
requires <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">x.compareTo(y) == -y.compareTo(x)</code> for all <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">x</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">y</code>. If <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">x</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">y</code>
are different types, this behaviour can’t be guaranteed.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComparableType")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ComparingThisWithNull<br>
            <small>this == null is always false, this != null is always true</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The boolean expression this != null always returns true and similarly this == null always returns false.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComparingThisWithNull")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ComparisonOutOfRange<br>
            <small>Comparison to value that is out of range for the compared type</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This checker looks for comparisons to values that are too high or too low for the compared type.  For example, bytes may have a value in the range -128 to 127. Comparing a byte for equality with a value outside that range will always evaluate to false and usually indicates an error in the code.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComparisonOutOfRange")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            CompatibleWithAnnotationMisuse<br>
            <small>@CompatibleWith's value is not a type argument.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CompatibleWith</code> annotation is used to mark parameters that need extra type
checking on arguments passed to the method. The annotation was not appropriately
placed on a parameter with a valid type argument. See the javadoc for more
details.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CompatibleWithAnnotationMisuse")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            CompileTimeConstant<br>
            <small>Non-compile-time constant expression passed to parameter with @CompileTimeConstant type annotation.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A method or constructor with one or more parameters whose declaration is
annotated with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CompileTimeConstant</code> type annotation must only be invoked
with corresponding actual parameters that are computed as compile-time constant
expressions, specifically expressions that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the Java compiler can determine a constant value for at compile time (see
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se11/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.28">JLS §15.28</a>),
or</li>
  <li>consist of the literal {@code null}, or</li>
  <li>consist of a single identifier, where the identifier is a formal method
parameter or class field that is effectively final and has the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CompileTimeConstant</code> annotation, or</li>
  <li>are ternary expressions with both branches being compile-time constants, or</li>
  <li>are formed from the concatenation of other compile time constant <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code>s,
or</li>
  <li>are Guava immutable collection factories with compile-time constant entries.</li>
</ul>

<p>For example, the following are valid compile-time constants:</p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"some literal string"</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"literal string" + compileTimeConstantParameter</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">debug ? compileTimeConstantParameter : "foo"</code></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList.of("a", "b", "c")</code></li>
</ul>

<p>When applied to fields, this check enforces that the field is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> and has an
initializer which satisfies the above conditions.</p>

<p>Getting Java 8 references to methods with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CompileTimeConstant</code> parameters is
disallowed because we couldn’t check if the method reference is later applied to
a compile-time constant. Use the methods directly instead.</p>

<p>For the same reason, it’s also disallowed to create lambda expressions with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CompileTimeConstant</code> parameters.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CompileTimeConstant")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ComputeIfAbsentAmbiguousReference<br>
            <small>computeIfAbsent passes the map key to the provided class's constructor</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>With ambiguous constructor references used in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Map#computeIfAbsent</code>
function parameter, it becomes unclear what the code intends to do.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">computeIfAbsent</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">someLong</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nl">AtomicLong:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="k">new</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">incrementAndGet</span><span class="o">()</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Code of this form can seemingly look like it’s trying to make a counter,
creating the key if absent. Unfortunately the code is surprising, because it
will call the wrong <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AtomicLong</code> constructor. Instead, it will create the
counter initialized with the key value, which is probably not desired.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComputeIfAbsentAmbiguousReference")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ConditionalExpressionNumericPromotion<br>
            <small>A conditional expression with numeric operands of differing types will perform binary numeric promotion of the operands; when these operands are of reference types, the expression's result may not be of the expected type.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A conditional expression with numeric second and third operands of differing
types may give surprising results.</p>

<p>For example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Object t = true ? Double.valueOf(0) : Integer.valueOf(0);
System.out.println(t.getClass());  // class java.lang.Double

Object f = false ? Double.valueOf(0) : Integer.valueOf(0);
System.out.println(f.getClass());  // class java.lang.Double !!
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Despite the apparent intent to get a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Double</code> in one case, and an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer</code> in
the other, the result is a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Double</code> in both cases.</p>

<p>This is because the rules in
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se9/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.25.2">JLS § 15.25.2</a>
state that differing numeric types will undergo binary numeric promotion. As
such, the latter case is evaluated as:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Object f =
    Double.valueOf(
        false
            ? Double.valueOf(0).doubleValue()
            : (double) Integer.valueOf(0).intValue());
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To get a different type in the two cases, one can either explicitly cast the
operands to a non-boxable type:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Object f = false ? ((Object) Double.valueOf(0)) : ((Object) Integer.valueOf(0));
System.out.println(t.getClass());  // class java.lang.Integer
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Or use if/else:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Object f;
if (false) {
  f = Double.valueOf(0);
} else {
  f = Integer.valueOf(0);
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ConditionalExpressionNumericPromotion")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ConstantOverflow<br>
            <small>Compile-time constant expression overflows</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Compile-time constant expressions that overflow are a potential source of bugs.</p>

<p>Literals without an explicit <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">L</code> suffix have type <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code>, so the following
multiplication expression is evaluated as an integer before being widened to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long</code>. The value is greater than <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer.MAX_VALUE</code>, so it wraps around to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-1857093632</code>.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">long</span> <span class="no">NANOS_PER_DAY</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">24</span>  <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The intent was probably for the multiplication expression to be evaluated as a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long</code> instead of an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code>.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">long</span> <span class="no">NANOS_PER_DAY</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">24L</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If you find yourself doing this kind of time-based math, consider using an API
that provides a safer, more readable and strongly-typed solution like the
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/time/Duration.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time.Duration</code></a>
API.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ConstantOverflow")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            DaggerProvidesNull<br>
            <small>Dagger @Provides methods may not return null unless annotated with @Nullable</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Dagger <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Provides</code> methods may not return null unless annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code>. Such a method will cause a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NullPointerException</code> at runtime if the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return null</code> path is ever taken.</p>

<p>If you believe the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return null</code> path can never be taken, please throw a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">RuntimeException</code> instead. Otherwise, please annotate the method with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DaggerProvidesNull")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

<p><em>Alternate names: ThrowableInstanceNeverThrown</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The exception is created with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">new</code>, but is not thrown, and the reference is
lost.</p>

<p>Creating an exception without using it is unlikely to be correct, so we assume
that you wanted to throw the exception.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DeadException")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This check prevents calls to methods annotated with Error Prone’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@DoNotCall</code>
annotation (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations.DoNotCall</code>).</p>

<p>The check disallows invocations and method references of the annotated method.</p>

<p>There are a few situations where this can be useful, including methods that are
required to satisfy the contract of an interface, but that are not supported.</p>

<p>A method annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@DoNotCall</code> should always be <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">abstract</code>. If
an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">abstract</code> method is annotated <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@DoNotCall</code> Error Prone will ensure all
implementations of that method also have the annotation. Methods annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@DoNotCall</code> should <em>not</em> be private, since a private method that should not be
called can simply be removed.</p>

<p>TIP: Marking methods annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@DoNotCall</code> as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Deprecated</code> is
recommended, since it provides IDE users with more immediate feedback.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Collection#add</code> should never be called on an immutable collection
implementation:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kn">package</span> <span class="nn">com.google.common.collect.ImmutableList</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">E</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="kd">implements</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">E</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="o">{</span>

 <span class="c1">// ...</span>

 <span class="cm">/**
  * Guaranteed to throw an exception and leave the list unmodified.
  *
  * @deprecated Unsupported operation.
  */</span>
 <span class="nd">@Deprecated</span>
 <span class="nd">@DoNotCall</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"guaranteed to throw an exception and leave the list unmodified"</span><span class="o">)</span>
 <span class="nd">@Override</span>
 <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="no">E</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
   <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">UnsupportedOperationException</span><span class="o">();</span>
 <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DoNotCall")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DoubleBraceInitialization<br>
            <small>Prefer collection factory methods or builders to the double-brace initialization pattern.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1958636/what-is-double-brace-initialization-in-java">double-brace initialization pattern</a> should be avoided—especially in
non-static contexts.</p>

<p>The double-brace pattern uses an instance-initializer in an anonymous inner
class to express the initialization of a class (often a collection) in a single
step.</p>

<p>Inner classes in a non-static context are terrific sources of memory leaks! If
you pass the collection somewhere that retains it, the entire instance you
created it from can no longer be garbage collected. Even if it is completely
unreachable. And if someone serializes the map? Yep, the entire creating
instance goes along for the ride (or if that fails, serializing the map fails,
which is also awfully strange). All this is completely nonobvious.</p>

<p>Luckily, there are more readable and more performant alternatives in the factory
methods and builders for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableMap</code>.</p>

<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List.of</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set.of</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map.of</code> static factories
<a href="https://openjdk.java.net/jeps/269">added in Java 9</a> are also a good choice.</p>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Denmark"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"Norway"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"Sweden"</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Not this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">ArrayList</span><span class="o">&lt;&gt;()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Denmark"</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="n">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Norway"</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="n">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Sweden"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">};</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>TIP: Neither the guava immutable collections nor the static factory methods
added in a JDK 9 support <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> elements. The double-brace pattern is still best
avoided for collections that contain null. Consider using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Arrays.asList</code> to
initialize <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code>s and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>s with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> values, and refactoring <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code>
initializers into a helper method.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DoubleBraceInitialization")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DuplicateMapKeys<br>
            <small>Map#ofEntries will throw an IllegalArgumentException if there are any duplicate keys</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>JDK 9 has
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/util/Map.html#ofEntries-java.util.Map.Entry...-"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map#ofEntries</code></a>
factory which throws runtime error when provided multiple entries with the same
key.</p>

<p>For eg, the following code is erroneously adding two entries with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo</code> as key.</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Map&lt;String, String&gt; map = Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("Foo", "Bar"),
    Map.entry("Ping", "Pong"),
    Map.entry("Kit", "Kat"),
    Map.entry("Foo", "Bar"));
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DuplicateMapKeys")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

            DurationFrom<br>
            <small>Duration.from(Duration) returns itself; from(Period) throws a runtime exception.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>

*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Duration.from(TemporalAmount) will always throw a UnsupportedTemporalTypeException when passed a Period and return itself when passed a Duration.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DurationFrom")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            DurationGetTemporalUnit<br>
            <small>Duration.get() only works with SECONDS or NANOS.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Duration.get(TemporalUnit)</code> only works when passed <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ChronoUnit.SECONDS</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ChronoUnit.NANOS</code>. All other values are guaranteed to throw a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">UnsupportedTemporalTypeException</code>. In general, you should avoid <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.get(ChronoUnit)</code>. Instead, please use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.toNanos()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Durations.toMicros(duration)</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.toMillis()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.getSeconds()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.toMinutes()</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.toHours()</code>, or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">duration.toDays()</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DurationGetTemporalUnit")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            DurationTemporalUnit<br>
            <small>Duration APIs only work for DAYS or exact durations.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Duration APIs only work for TemporalUnits with exact durations or ChronoUnit.DAYS. E.g., Duration.of(1, ChronoUnit.YEARS) is guaranteed to throw a DateTimeException.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DurationTemporalUnit")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            EqualsHashCode<br>
            <small>Classes that override equals should also override hashCode.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The contract for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.hashCode</code> states that if two objects are equal, then
calling the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code> method on each of the two objects must produce the same
result. Implementing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code> but not <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code> causes broken behaviour
when trying to store the object in a collection.</p>

<p>See <a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=BIpDDwAAQBAJ">Effective Java 3rd Edition §11</a> for more information and a
discussion of how to correctly implement <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("EqualsHashCode")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            EqualsNaN<br>
            <small>== NaN always returns false; use the isNaN methods instead</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>As per JLS 15.21.1, == NaN comparisons always return false, even NaN == NaN.
Instead, use the isNaN methods to check for NaN.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("EqualsNaN")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>
