        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            CloseableProvides<br>
            <small>Providing Closeable resources makes their lifecycle unclear</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>If you provide
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/io/Closeable.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Closeable</code></a>
resources through dependency injection, it can be difficult to effectively
manage the lifecycle of the Closable:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">MyModule</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nf">AbstractModule</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@Provides</span>
  <span class="nc">FileOutputStream</span> <span class="nf">provideFileStream</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">FileOutputStream</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"/tmp/outfile"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="o">...</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Client</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">FileOutputStream</span> <span class="n">fos</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">Client</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">FileOutputStream</span> <span class="n">fos</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">OtherDependency</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">...)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
     <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">fos</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">fos</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="kd">throws</span> <span class="nc">IOException</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">fos</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">write</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello!"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>There are a number of issues with this approach as it relates to resource
management:</p>

<ul>
  <li>If multiple Client classes are constructed, multiple output streams are
opened against the same file, and writes to the file may clash with each
other.</li>
  <li>
    <p>It’s not clear which class has the responsibility of closing the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FileOutputStream</code> resource:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>If the resource is created for the sole ownership of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Client</code>, then it
makes sense for the client to close it.</li>
      <li>However, if the resource is scoped (e.g.: you add <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Singleton</code> to the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Provides</code> method), then suddenly it’s <em>not</em> the responsibility of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Client</code> to close the resource. If one <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Client</code> closes the stream, then
all of the other users of that stream will be dealing with a closed
resource. There needs to be some other ‘resource manager’ object that
also gets that stream, and its closing functions are call in the right
place. That can be tricky to do correctly.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>If, for example, the construction of the other dependencies of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Client</code>
fails (resulting in a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ProvisionException</code>), then the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FileOutputStream</code>
that may have been constructed leaks and isn’t properly closed, even if
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Client</code> normally closes its resources correctly.</li>
</ul>

<p>The preferred solution is to not inject closable resources, but instead, objects
that can expose short-lived closable resources that are used as necessary. The
following example uses Guava’s
<a href="https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/IOExplained#sources-and-sinks">CharSink</a>
as the resource manager object:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">MyModule</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nf">AbstractModule</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@Provides</span>
  <span class="nc">CharSink</span> <span class="nf">provideCharSink</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">Files</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">asCharSink</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">File</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"/tmp/outfile"</span><span class="o">),</span> <span class="nc">StandardCharsets</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">UTF_8</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="o">...</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Client</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">CharSink</span> <span class="n">sink</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">Client</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">CharSink</span> <span class="n">sink</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">OtherDependency</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">...)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
     <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">sink</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">sink</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="kd">throws</span> <span class="nc">IOException</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">sink</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">write</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello!"</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// Opens the file at this point, and closes once its done.</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If there’s not a similar non-closable resource, you can write a simple wrapper:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">ResourceManager</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">ResourceManager</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nd">@Config</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">configs</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">...)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>

  <span class="cm">/**
   * Returns a new thing for you to use and dispose of
   */</span>
  <span class="nc">OutputStream</span> <span class="nf">provideInstance</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span><span class="o">...();</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Client</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ResourceManager</span> <span class="n">resource</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">Client</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ResourceManager</span> <span class="n">resource</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">OtherDependency</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">...)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
     <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">resource</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">resource</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">OutputStream</span> <span class="n">actualStream</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">resource</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">provideInstance</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="c1">// write to actualStream, closing with try-with-resources</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This pattern can be extended to other resources: as opposed to injecting
database connection handles directly, inject connection pool objects that
require your object to ask for those connection objects when they’re needed and
close them safely.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CloseableProvides")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ClosingStandardOutputStreams<br>
            <small>Don't use try-with-resources to manage standard output streams, closing the stream will cause subsequent output to standard output or standard error to be lost</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Closing the standard output streams <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.out</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.err</code> will cause all
subsequent standard output to be dropped, including stack traces from exceptions
that propagate to the top level.</p>

<p>Avoid using try-with-resources to manage <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">PrintWriter</code>s or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">OutputStream</code>s that
wrap <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.out</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.err</code>, since the try-with-resource statement will
close the underlying streams.</p>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(System.err));
pw.println("hello");
pw.flush();
</code></pre>

<p>Instead of this:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">try (PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(System.err))) {
  pw.println("hello");
}
</code></pre>

<p>Consider the following example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>import java.io.OutputStreamWriter;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

public class X {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.err.println("one");
    try (PrintWriter err = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(System.err, UTF_8))) {
      err.print("two");
    }
    // System.err has been closed, no more output will be printed!
    System.err.println("three");
    throw new AssertionError();
  }
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The program will print the following, and return with exit code 1. Note that the
last <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">println</code> doesn’t produce any output, and the exception’s stack trace is
not printed:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>one
two
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ClosingStandardOutputStreams")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            CollectionUndefinedEquality<br>
            <small>This type does not have well-defined equals behavior.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection</code>s (and other types which rely on equality) to contain elements
with undefined equality is error-prone. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection</code> itself does
not have well-defined equality: the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code> subinterfaces are not
necessarily comparable.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Collection</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;&gt;</span> <span class="n">collectionsOfIntegers</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ImmutableSet</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">),</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableSet</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">4</span><span class="o">));</span>

<span class="n">collectionsOfIntegers</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">contains</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ImmutableSet</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">));</span> <span class="c1">// true</span>
<span class="n">collectionsOfIntegers</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">contains</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">));</span> <span class="c1">// false</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">containsTest</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Collection</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">CharSequence</span><span class="o">&gt;&gt;</span> <span class="n">charSequences</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// True if `charSequences` actually contains Strings, but otherwise not necessarily.</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">charSequences</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">contains</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"test"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>In this case, an appropriate fix may be,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">containsTest</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Collection</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">CharSequence</span><span class="o">&gt;&gt;</span> <span class="n">charSequences</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">charSequences</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">stream</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">anyMatch</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"test"</span><span class="o">::</span><span class="n">contentEquals</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CollectionUndefinedEquality")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ComparableAndComparator<br>
            <small>Class should not implement both `Comparable` and `Comparator`</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparator</code> is an object that knows how to compare other objects, whereas an
object implementing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparable</code> knows how to compare itself to other objects of
the same type.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComparableAndComparator")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            CompareToZero<br>
            <small>The result of #compareTo or #compare should only be compared to 0. It is an implementation detail whether a given type returns strictly the values {-1, 0, +1} or others.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The contract for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparator#compare</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Comparable#compareTo</code> states that the
result is an integer which is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&lt; 0</code> for less than, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">== 0</code> for equality and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&gt; 0</code>
for greater than. While most implementations return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-1</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">+1</code> for those
cases respectively, this is not guaranteed. Always comparing to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code> is the
safest use of the return value.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">isLessThan</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Comparator</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="c1">// Fragile: it's not guaranteed that `comparator` returns -1 to mean</span>
    <span class="c1">// "less than".</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compare</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="o">-</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">isLessThan</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Comparator</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compare</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Even comparisons which are otherwise correct are clearer to other readers of the
code if turned into a comparison to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code>, e.g.:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">greaterThan</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Comparator</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compare</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">&gt;=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">greaterThan</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Comparator</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">T</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">T</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">comparator</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compare</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CompareToZero")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ComplexBooleanConstant<br>
            <small>Non-trivial compile time constant boolean expressions shouldn't be used.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When a boolean expression is a compile-time constant (e.g.: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">2 &lt; 1</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">1 == 1</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">'a' &lt; 'A'</code>), these expressions can be directly replaced with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">true</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">false</code>,
as appropriate. In any context where these expressions are used, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">true</code> or
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">false</code> is a more readable alternative:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">2</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Some code I don't want to run right now</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Some loop that I will manually break out of</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="k">assert</span> <span class="mi">1</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="c1">// I want to force an AssertionFailure if assertions are enabled</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Some code I don't want to run right now</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Some loop that I will manually break out of</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="k">assert</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="c1">// I want to force an AssertionFailure if assertions are enabled</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>When some boolean expression is a compile-time constant unexpectedly, it
generally represents a bug in the code:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">100</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="n">i</span><span class="o">++)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">out</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Is "</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">" greater than 50?: "</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span> <span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="mi">50</span><span class="o">));</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="c1">// Prints "... false" 100 times, since i &gt; 50 is mistyped as 1 &gt; 50</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComplexBooleanConstant")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DateChecker<br>
            <small>Warns against suspect looking calls to java.util.Date APIs</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>java.util.Date uses 1900-based years, 0-based months, 1-based days, and 0-based hours/minutes/seconds. Additionally, it allows for negative values or very large values (which rollover).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DateChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            DateFormatConstant<br>
            <small>DateFormat is not thread-safe, and should not be used as a constant field.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/text/DateFormat.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateFormat</code></a> is not thread-safe. The documentation recommends creating
separate format instances for each thread. If multiple threads access a format
concurrently, it must be synchronized externally.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s5.2.4-constant-names">Google Java Style Guide §5.2.4</a> requires <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">CONSTANT_CASE</code> to only be
used for static final fields whose contents are deeply immutable and whose
methods have no detectable side effects, so fields of type <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateFormat</code> should
not use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">CONSTANT_CASE</code>.</p>

<p>TIP: Consider using the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time</code> API added in Java8, in particular
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/time/format/DateTimeFormatter.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateTimeFormatter</code></a>. One its many advantages over <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateFormat</code> is that it is
immutable and thread-safe.</p>

<p>If the date formatter is accessed by multiple threads, consider using
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/ThreadLocal.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code></a>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DateFormat</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="no">DATE_FORMAT</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">withInitial</span><span class="o">(()</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">SimpleDateFormat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm"</span><span class="o">));</span>

</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If the field is never accessed by multiple threads, rename it to use
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">lowerCamelCase</code>.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// not thread safe</span>
<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">DateFormat</span> <span class="n">dateFormat</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">SimpleDateFormat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm"</span><span class="o">);</span>

</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DateFormatConstant")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            DeeplyNested<br>
            <small>Very deeply nested code may lead to StackOverflowErrors during compilation</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Having an extremely long Java statement with many chained method calls can cause
compilation to fail with a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">StackOverflowError</code> when the compiler tries to
recursively process it.</p>

<p>This is a common problem in generated code.</p>

<p>As an alternative to extremely long chained method calls, e.g. for builders,
consider something like the following for collections with hundreds or thousands
of entries:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="no">FEATURES</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">createFeatures</span><span class="o">();</span>

<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">createFeatures</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">builder</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"bar"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>over code like this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="no">FEATURES</span> <span class="o">=</span>
  <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">()</span>
    <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">)</span>
    <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"bar"</span><span class="o">)</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
    <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DeeplyNested")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            DefaultCharset<br>
            <small>Implicit use of the platform default charset, which can result in differing behaviour between JVM executions or incorrect behavior if the encoding of the data source doesn't match expectations.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/nio/charset/Charset.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Charset</code></a> is a mapping between sequences of
<a href="https://unicode.org/glossary/#code_unit">16-bit Unicode code units</a> and sequences of bytes. Charsets are used
when encoding characters into bytes and decoding bytes into characters.</p>

<p>Using APIs that rely on the JVM’s default Charset under the hood is dangerous.
The default charset can vary from machine to machine or JVM to JVM. This can
lead to unstable character encoding/decoding between runs of your program, even
for ASCII characters (e.g.: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">A</code> is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0100 0001</code> in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">UTF-8</code>, but is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0000 0000
0100 0001</code> in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">UTF-16</code>).</p>

<p>If you need stable encoding/decoding, you must specify an explicit charset. The
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/nio/charset/StandardCharsets.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">StandardCharsets</code></a> class provides these constants for you.</p>

<p>When in doubt, use <a href="https://www.utf8everywhere.org/">UTF-8</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DefaultCharset")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DeprecatedVariable<br>
            <small>Applying the @Deprecated annotation to local variables or parameters has no effect</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Deprecated</code> annotations should not be applied to local variables and
parameters, since they have no effect there.</p>

<p>The
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Deprecated.html">javadoc for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Deprecated</code></a>
says</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Use of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Deprecated</code> annotation on a local variable declaration or on a
parameter declaration or a package declaration has no effect on the warnings
issued by a compiler.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DeprecatedVariable")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            DirectInvocationOnMock<br>
            <small>Methods should not be directly invoked on mocks. Should this be part of a verify(..) call?</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Direct invocations on <a href="https://site.mockito.org/">mocks</a> should be avoided in tests.</p>

<p>When you call a method on a mock, the call normally does only what you have
configured it to do (through calls to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">when(...).thenReturn/thenAnswer</code>, etc.)
and makes a record of the call that can be read by later <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">verify(...)</code> calls.
Both of these are rarely what you want:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The reason to configure a mock’s behavior is so that the code under test
will react to that behavior. If you want for the test itself to do
something, then do it directly instead of by calling a method on the mock.</li>
  <li>If a future reader of your test sees a call to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">verify(foo).bar()</code>, then the
reader will expect the test to succeed only because the code under test
called <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">bar()</code>, not because the test itself did.</li>
</ul>

<p>Sometimes, test authors, especially those familiar with other mocking frameworks
(like EasyMock), will call a method on a mock for one of two reasons:</p>

<ol>
  <li>By default, EasyMock requires the test setup to call every method that the
code under test will call. Mockito’s defaults do <em>not</em> require this.</li>
  <li>Many EasyMock tests choose to have EasyMock require that the code under test
call <em>all</em> the methods that the test setup calls. Mockito tests that want to
verify calls to methods must verify each call individually. To check that
any particular method has been called, a Mockito test must call
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">verify(foo).bar()</code>, and it must do so <em>after</em> the code under test has run.</li>
</ol>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">balanceIsChecked</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">Account</span> <span class="n">account</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">mock</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Account</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="nc">LoanChecker</span> <span class="n">loanChecker</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">LoanChecker</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">account</span><span class="o">);</span>

  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">loanChecker</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">checkEligibility</span><span class="o">()).</span><span class="na">isFalse</span><span class="o">();</span>

  <span class="c1">// Should be verify(account).checkBalance();, or be removed if the call to</span>
  <span class="c1">// `checkEligibility` is sufficient proof the code is behaving as intended.</span>
  <span class="n">account</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">checkBalance</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>There is at least one edge case in which a call to a mock has different effects:
A call to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> method will normally <em>not</em> be intercepted by Mockito, so it
will run the implementation of that method in the code under test. Sometimes,
that method will call other methods on the mock object, producing effects
similar to if the test had called those methods directly. Sometimes, the method
will have other effects. Both kinds of effects can be confusing, so prefer to
avoid such calls when possible.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DirectInvocationOnMock")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            DistinctVarargsChecker<br>
            <small>Method expects distinct arguments at some/all positions</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Various methods which take variable-length arguments throw runtime exceptions
like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IllegalArgumentException</code> when the arguments are not distinct.</p>

<p>This checker warns on using non-distinct parameters in various varargs methods
when the usage is either redundant or will result in a runtime exception.</p>

<p>Bad:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableSet</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">first</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">third</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Good:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableSet</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">first</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">third</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DistinctVarargsChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DoNotClaimAnnotations<br>
            <small>Don't 'claim' annotations in annotation processors; Processor#process should unconditionally return `false`</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Do not ‘claim’ annotations in annotation processors; <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.compiler/javax/annotation/processing/Processor.html#process(java.util.Set,javax.annotation.processing.RoundEnvironment)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Processor#process</code></a>
should unconditionally <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return false</code>. Claiming annotations prevents other
processors from seeing the annotations, which there’s usually no reason to do.
It’s also fragile, since it relies on the order the processors run in, and
there’s no robust way in most build systems to ensure a particular processor
sees the annotations first.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DoNotClaimAnnotations")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DoNotMockAutoValue<br>
            <small>AutoValue classes represent pure data classes, so mocking them should not be necessary. Construct a real instance of the class instead.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> is used to represent pure data classes. Mocking these should not be
necessary: prefer constructing them in the same way production code would.</p>

<p>To make the argument another way: the fact that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AutoValue</code> classes are not
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> is an implementation detail of the way they’re generated. They should be
regarded as logically final insofar as they must not be extended by
non-generated code. If they were final, they also would not be mockable.</p>

<p>Instead of mocking:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span> <span class="n">myAutoValue</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">mock</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">when</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">myAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getFoo</span><span class="o">()).</span><span class="na">thenReturn</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Prefer simply constructing an instance:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span> <span class="n">myAutoValue</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">create</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If your <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AutoValue</code> has multiple required fields, and only one is relevant for a
test, consider using a <a href="https://github.com/google/auto/blob/master/value/userguide/builders.md">builder</a> or <a href="https://github.com/google/auto/blob/master/value/userguide/builders-howto.md#withers"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">with</code>-style methods</a> to create
test instances with just the fields you care about. Consider using</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span> <span class="nf">myAutoValueBuilder</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">bar</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">42</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">baz</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span> <span class="n">myAutoValue</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">myAutoValueBuilder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>or:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span> <span class="no">MY_AUTO_VALUE</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">create</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="cm">/* foo= */</span> <span class="s">""</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="cm">/* bar= */</span> <span class="mi">42</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="cm">/* baz= */</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">);</span>

<span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyAutoValue</span> <span class="n">myAutoValue</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="no">MY_AUTO_VALUE</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">withFoo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"foo"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DoNotMockAutoValue")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            DoubleCheckedLocking<br>
            <small>Double-checked locking on non-volatile fields is unsafe</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using double-checked locking on mutable objects in non-volatile fields is not
thread-safe.</p>

<p>If the field is not volatile, the compiler may re-order the code in the
accessor. For more information, see:</p>

<ul>
  <li>https://jeremymanson.blogspot.com/2008/05/double-checked-locking.html</li>
  <li>https://www.cs.umd.edu/~pugh/java/memoryModel/DoubleCheckedLocking.html</li>
  <li>Java Concurrency in Practice, §16.2.4</li>
  <li><a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=BIpDDwAAQBAJ">Effective Java 3rd Edition §83</a></li>
</ul>

<p>The canonical example of <em>correct</em> double-checked locking for lazy
initialization is:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="cm">/** This foo's bar.  Lazily initialized via double-checked locking. */</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">volatile</span> <span class="nc">Bar</span> <span class="n">bar</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">Bar</span> <span class="nf">getBar</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Bar</span> <span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">bar</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
        <span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">bar</span><span class="o">;</span>
        <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
          <span class="n">bar</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">value</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">computeBar</span><span class="o">();</span>
        <span class="o">}</span>
      <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">value</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="nc">Bar</span> <span class="nf">computeBar</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<!--
  TODO: Consider instead:
  - moving the synchronized block into a separate method to encourage getBar inlining
  - using (sharper) jdk9+ VarHandle.getAcquire together with VarHandle.setRelease
  - Suppliers.memoize
  - AtomicReference.updateAndGet()
-->

<h2 id="alternatives">Alternatives</h2>

<p>Double-checked locking should only be used in performance critical classes. For
code that is less performance sensitive, there are simpler, more readable
approaches. Effective Java recommends two alternatives:</p>

<h3 id="synchronized-accessors">Synchronized Accessors</h3>

<p>For lazily initializing instance fields, consider a <em>synchronized accessor</em>. In
modern JVMs with efficient uncontended synchronization the performance
difference is often negligible.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// Lazy initialization of instance field - synchronized accessor</span>
<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">field</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="nf">get</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">field</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">field</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">computeValue</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">field</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h3 id="holder-classes">Holder Classes</h3>

<p>If the field being initialized is static, consider using the <em>lazy
initialization holder class</em> idiom:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// Lazy initialization holder class idiom for static fields</span>
<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Holder</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">field</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">computeValue</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
<span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="nf">get</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">Holder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">field</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="double-checked-locking-and-immutability">Double-checked locking and immutability</h2>

<p>If the object being initialized with double-checked locking is
<a href="https://jeremymanson.blogspot.com/2008/04/immutability-in-java.html">immutable</a>,
then it is safe for the field to be non-volatile. <em>However</em>, the use of volatile
is still encouraged because it is almost free on x86 and makes the code more
obviously correct.</p>

<p>Note that immutable has a very specific meaning in this context:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>[An immutable object] is transitively reachable from a final field, has not
changed since the final field was set, and a reference to the object
containing the final field did not escape the constructor.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Double-checked locking on non-volatile fields is in general unsafe because the
compiler and JVM can re-order code from the object’s constructor to occur
<em>after</em> the object is written to the field.</p>

<p>The final modifier prevents that re-ordering from occurring, and guarantees that
all of the object’s final fields have been written to before a reference to that
object is published.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DoubleCheckedLocking")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            DuplicateBranches<br>
            <small>Both branches contain identical code</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Branching constructs (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> statements, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">conditional</code> expressions) should contain
difference code in the two branches. Repeating identical code in both branches
is usually a bug.</p>

<p>For example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">condition</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">same</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">same</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">condition</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">same</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">else</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">same</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>this usually indicates a typo where one of the branches was supposed to contain
different logic:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">condition</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">something</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">somethingElse</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">condition</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">doSomething</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">else</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">doSomethingElse</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("DuplicateBranches")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <a href="/docs/installation">Docs</a>
      </li>
      <li><a href="https://github.com/google/error-prone">GitHub</a></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
</nav>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            EmptyCatch<br>
            <small>Caught exceptions should not be ignored</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Style</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <a href="https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s6.2-caught-exceptions">Google Java Style Guide §6.2</a> states:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>It is very rarely correct to do nothing in response to a caught exception.
(Typical responses are to log it, or if it is considered “impossible”, rethrow
it as an AssertionError.)</p>

  <p>When it truly is appropriate to take no action whatsoever in a catch block,
the reason this is justified is explained in a comment.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>When writing tests that expect an exception to be thrown, prefer using
<a href="https://junit.org/junit4/javadoc/latest/org/junit/Assert.html#assertThrows(java.lang.Class,%20org.junit.function.ThrowingRunnable)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Assert.assertThrows</code></a> instead of writing a try-catch. That is,
prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">assertThrows</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">NoSuchElementException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">emptyStack</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">pop</span><span class="o">());</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>instead of this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">emptyStack</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">pop</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">fail</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">NoSuchElementException</span> <span class="n">expected</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>


    </div>

          <h1>
            EmptySetMultibindingContributions<br>
            <small>@Multibinds is a more efficient and declarative mechanism for ensuring that a set multibinding is present in the graph.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When using <a href="https://dagger.dev/multibindings.html">Dagger Multibinding</a>, you can use methods like the below to
make sure that there’s a (potentially empty) Set binding for your type:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Provides</span> <span class="nd">@ElementsIntoSet</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">MyType</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">provideEmptySetOfMyType</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">HashSet</span><span class="o">&lt;&gt;();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>However, there’s a slightly easier way to express this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Multibinds</span> <span class="kd">abstract</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">MyType</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">provideEmptySetOfMyType</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("EmptySetMultibindingContributions")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

            EmptyTopLevelDeclaration<br>
            <small>Empty top-level type declarations should be omitted</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>

*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A semi-colon at the top level of a Java file is treated as an empty type
declaration in the grammar, but it’s confusing and unnecessary.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>

          <h1>
            EnumOrdinal<br>
            <small>You should almost never invoke the Enum.ordinal() method or depend on the enum values by index.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>You should almost never invoke the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Enum.ordinal()</code> method, nor depend on some
enum constant being at a particular index of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">values()</code> array. The ordinal
of a given enum value is not guaranteed to be stable across builds because of
the potential for enum values to be added, removed, or reordered. The ordinal
exists only to support low-level utilities like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">EnumSet</code>.</p>

<p>Prefer using enum value directly:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableMap</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="no">MAPPING</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">ImmutableMap</span><span class="o">.&lt;</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">()</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">put</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">FOO</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"Foo"</span><span class="o">)</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">put</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">BAR</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"Bar"</span><span class="o">)</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">buildOrThrow</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>instead of relying on the ordinal:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">ImmutableMap</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="no">MAPPING</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">ImmutableMap</span><span class="o">.&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">()</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">put</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">FOO</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">ordinal</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="s">"Foo"</span><span class="o">)</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">put</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyEnum</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">BAR</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">ordinal</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="s">"Bar"</span><span class="o">)</span>
        <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">buildOrThrow</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If you need a stable number for serialisation, consider defining an explicit
field on the enum:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="nc">MyStableEnum</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="no">FOO</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">),</span>
  <span class="no">BAR</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">),</span>
  <span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">wireCode</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="nc">MyStableEnum</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">wireCode</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">wireCode</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">wireCode</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>rather than relying on the ordinal values:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="nc">MyUnstableEnum</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="no">FOO</span><span class="o">,</span>
  <span class="no">BAR</span><span class="o">,</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
<span class="nc">MyUnstableEnum</span> <span class="nf">fromWire</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">wireCode</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">MyUnstableEnum</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">values</span><span class="o">()[</span><span class="n">wireCode</span><span class="o">];</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("EnumOrdinal")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>
