          <h1>
            IdentityHashMapUsage<br>
            <small>IdentityHashMap usage shouldn't be intermingled with Map</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.IdentityHashMap</code> uses reference equality to compare keys. This is
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/IdentityHashMap.html">in violation of the contract of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Map</code></a>,
which states that object equality (the keys’ <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> methods) should be used
for key comparison. This peculiarity can lead to confusion and subtle bugs,
especially when the two types of maps are used together. This check attempts to
reduce confusion between these two very different kinds of maps in a few ways:</p>

<ol>
  <li>An <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code>’s reference-equality behavior would be surprising if
its declared type was <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Map</code>. The type of an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code> is
required to be explicit, i.e., <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code> should not be upcast to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code>.</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code>’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> method will only compare equal to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code> if
the keys of both are the same instances. This makes little sense for an
object-equality map, so <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap.equals()</code> should only be used to
compare to other <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code>s.</li>
  <li>The semantics of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IdentityHashMap</code> are different enough that they
should be considered different, incompatible types. Converting one to the
other is discouraged, as it is often a mistake.</li>
</ol>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">bad</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">aMap</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">IdentityHashMap</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Don't assign an `IdentityHashMap` to a plain `Map`-typed variable</span>
  <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">myMap</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="c1">// Don't use `IdentityHashMap`'s `equals` method with a `Map`</span>
  <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">aMap</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="c1">// Don't convert between `IdentityHashMap` and `Map`</span>
  <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">putAll</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">aMap</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">identityMap</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">IdentityHashMap</span><span class="o">&lt;&gt;(</span><span class="n">aMap</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// Keep `IdentityHashMap`'s type information around so maintainers know when</span>
<span class="c1">// reference equality is being used.</span>
<span class="nc">IdentityHashMap</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">good</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">IdentityHashMap</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">identityMap</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">IdentityHashMap</span><span class="o">&lt;&gt;();</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">identityMap</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IdentityHashMapUsage")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            IfChainToSwitch<br>
            <small>This if-chain may be converted into a switch</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>We’re trying to make long chains of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> statements clearer (and potentially
faster) by converting them into <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es.</p>

<h3 id="long-chains-of-if-statements">Long chains of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> statements</h3>

<ul>
  <li>When a chain of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if ... else if ... else if ...</code> statements has <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">K</code> total
branches, at runtime one needs to check <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">O(K)</code> conditions on average
(assuming equal likelihood of each branch)</li>
  <li>Condition-checking expressions are often repeated multiple times, once in
each <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if (...)</code>. Besides redundancy, this introduces a potential bug vector:
an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> in the chain could unintentionally have a slightly different
condition than others, an ordering bug (see below), <em>etc.</em></li>
</ul>

<h3 id="switches"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>Support constants (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">1</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">2</code>, …), <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">enum</code> values, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>, and pattern
matching, including mixtures of these</li>
  <li>Reduces redundancy</li>
  <li>Runtime performance may benefit</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="examples">Examples</h3>

<h4 id="1-enum-conversion">1. Enum conversion</h4>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void foo(Suit suit) {
  if (suit == Suit.SPADE) {
    System.out.println("spade");
  } else if (suit == Suit.HEART || suit == Suit.DIAMOND) {
    System.out.println("red suit");
  } else if (suit == Suit.CLUB) {
    System.out.println("club");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>Which can be converted into:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void foo(Suit suit) {
  switch (suit) {
    case Suit.SPADE -&gt; System.out.println("spade");
    case Suit.HEART, Suit.DIAMOND -&gt; System.out.println("red suit");
    case Suit.CLUB -&gt; System.out.println("club");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>If the flag <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-XepOpt:IfChainToSwitch:EnableSafe=true</code> is set, the output will
include an empty <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case null</code>; this more closely matches the behavior of the
original if-chain when <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">suit</code> is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>, although is more verbose and may not
match the intent.</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void foo(Suit suit) {
  switch (suit) {
    case Suit.SPADE -&gt; System.out.println("spade");
    case Suit.HEART, Suit.DIAMOND -&gt; System.out.println("red suit");
    case Suit.CLUB -&gt; System.out.println("club");
    case null -&gt; {}
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>Note that with the new <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> style (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-&gt;</code>), exhaustiveness checking is
provided by the compiler for ‘enhanced’ switch statements (see <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-14.html#jls-14.11.2">JLS §14.11.2</a>),
and for traditional switch statements by Error Prone
(https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/MissingCasesInEnumSwitch). That is, if a new <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Suit</code> value were to
be added to the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">enum</code>, then the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> would raise a compile-time error,
whereas the original chain of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> statements would need to be manually detected
and edited.</p>

<h4 id="2-patterns">2. Patterns</h4>

<p>This conversion works for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceof</code>s too:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void describeObject(Object obj) {

  if (obj instanceof String) {
    System.out.println("It's a string!");
  } else if (obj instanceof Number n) {
    System.out.println("It's a number!");
  } else if (obj instanceof Object) {
    System.out.println("It's an object!");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>This can be converted as follows (if the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceof</code> does not originally have a
pattern variable, then <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">unused</code> will be inserted):</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void describeObject(Object obj) {

  switch(obj) {
    case String unused -&gt; System.out.println("It's a string!");
    case Number n -&gt; System.out.println("It's a number!");
    case Object unused -&gt; System.out.println("It's an object!");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>In later Java versions, an unnamed variable (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">_</code>) can be used in place of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">unused</code>.</p>

<h4 id="3-ordering-bugs">3. Ordering Bugs</h4>

<p>With <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code> chains, it’s possible to write code such as:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">private void describeObject(Object obj) {

  if (obj instanceof Object) {
    System.out.println("It's an object!");
  } else if (obj instanceof Number n) {
    System.out.println("It's a number!");
  } else if (obj instanceof String) {
    System.out.println("It's a string!");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>When calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">describeObject("hello")</code>, one might expect to have <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">It's a
string!</code> printed, but this is not what happens. Because the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> check
happens first in code, it matches, resulting in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">It's an object!</code>. This behavior
is most likely a bug, and can sometimes be hard to spot. This checker will
automatically reorder <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s if needed to correct the issue, like this:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">private void describeObject(Object obj) {

  switch(obj) {
    case Number n -&gt; System.out.println("It's a number!");
    case String unused -&gt; System.out.println("It's a string!");
    case Object unused -&gt; System.out.println("It's an object!");
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>In this way, the behavior of the switch (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">It's a string!</code>) and the original
if-chain (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">It's an object!</code>) are different. To prevent the checker from changing
behavior in this way, set the flag <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-XepOpt:IfChainToSwitch:EnableSafe=true</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IfChainToSwitch")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            IgnoredPureGetter<br>
            <small>Getters on AutoValues, AutoBuilders, and Protobuf Messages are side-effect free, so there is no point in calling them if the return value is ignored. While there are no side effects from the getter, the receiver may have side effects.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IgnoredPureGetter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ImmutableAnnotationChecker<br>
            <small>Annotations should always be immutable</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>LikelyError</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: Immutable</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Annotations should always be immutable.</p>

<p>Static state is dangerous to begin with, but much worse for annotations.
Annotation instances are usually constants, and it is very surprising if their
state ever changes, or if they are not thread-safe.</p>

<p>TIP: prefer [<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoAnnotation</code>] to writing annotation implementations by hand.</p>

<p>To make annotation implementations immutable, ensure:</p>

<ul>
  <li>All fields are final.</li>
  <li>The types of all fields are deeply immutable. For example, use
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code> instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>.</li>
  <li>To signal to Error Prone that the type of a field is immutable, add
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations.Immutable</code> to its declaration.</li>
  <li>If the implementation is a member class, ensure it is static to avoid
capturing state from a mutable enclosing instance. If it is an anonymous
class, convert it to a named member class so it can be made static.</li>
</ul>

<p>TIP: annotating the declaration of an annotation with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Immutable</code> is
unnecessary – Error Prone assumes annotations are immutable by default.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ImmutableAnnotationChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ImmutableEnumChecker<br>
            <small>Enums should always be immutable</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: Immutable</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>All fields in your enum class should be final and either be primitive or refer
to deeply immutable objects.</p>

<p>Static state is dangerous to begin with, but much worse for enums. We all think
of enum values as constants – and even refer to them as “enum constants” – and
would be very surprised if any of their state ever changed, or was not
thread-safe.</p>

<p>To make enums immutable, ensure:</p>

<ul>
  <li>All fields are final.</li>
  <li>
    <p>The types of all fields of the enum are deeply immutable. For example, use
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code> instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p>Types are considered immutable if they are primitives, in a set of types
that are built in to Error Prone (e.g. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.lang.String</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.UUID</code>), or are annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations.Immutable</code>.</p>

        <p>Other versions of the annotation, such as
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.annotation.concurrent.Immutable</code>, are currently <em>not</em> recognized.
See https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/Immutable for additional discussion.</p>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p>If the type you’re using inside the enum can be annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Immutable</code>, you should do that:</p>

        <div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// WARNING: E is not immutable, since MyValueObject isn't Immutable</span>
<span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="no">E</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">MyValueObject</span> <span class="n">mvo</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">MyValueObject</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="c1">// Add @Immutable here</span>
<span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">MyValueObject</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
</code></pre></div>        </div>

        <p>Note that MyValueObject must actually be immutable. The
<a href="/bugpattern/Immutable.html">Immutable</a> checker will raise a compile-time error if the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">MyValueObject</code> class isn’t actually immutable.</p>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p>If the type you’re using inside the enum is not considered immutable,
and you can’t annotate the type because it’s outside the project,
consider using an immutable replacement of the type, or
<a href="#suppression">suppress this check on the enum</a> with a comment about why
the fields in question are immutable.</p>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>TIP: annotating the declaration of the enum class with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Immutable</code> is
unnecessary – Error Prone assumes enums are immutable by default.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kn">import</span> <span class="nn">com.google.errorprone.annotations.Immutable</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Immutable</span>
<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nf">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">id</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// The declaration doesn't need to be annotated with @Immutable.</span>
<span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="no">E</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="no">A</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"A"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">),</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">))),</span>
  <span class="no">B</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"B"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="o">)));</span>

  <span class="c1">// All fields are final, and deeply immutable:</span>
  <span class="c1">// Error Prone knows String is immutable.</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="c1">// Error Prone knows ImmutableList&lt;T&gt; is an immutable collection of some</span>
  <span class="c1">// objects, and it recognizes the @Immutable annotation on the declaration of</span>
  <span class="c1">// Foo, so it can safely determine that this ImmutableList is deeply</span>
  <span class="c1">// immutable.</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">foos</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="nf">E</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">foos</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">name</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">foos</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">foos</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">foos</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">foos</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="nf">name</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">foos</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>TIP: Instead of creating an enum with functional interface fields (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Predicate</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Function</code>, etc.), declare abstract methods that are overridden by each
constant. For example, do this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="nc">Types</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="no">STRING</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@Override</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">},</span>
  <span class="no">NUMBER</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@Override</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">},</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">abstract</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>… not this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">enum</span> <span class="nc">Types</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="no">STRING</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">),</span>
  <span class="no">NUMBER</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="o">),</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>

  <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Predicate</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Object</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="nc">Types</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Predicate</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Object</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasCompatibleType</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">hasCompatibleType</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This has several advantages on top of sidestepping this checker, e.g. not tying
you to a particular functional interface type – your callers should e.g. use
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">STRING::hasCompatibleType</code> instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">STRING.hasCompatibleType</code> which only
works for one interface type.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ImmutableEnumChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InconsistentCapitalization<br>
            <small>It is confusing to have a field and a parameter under the same scope that differ only in capitalization.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>It is confusing to have two or more variables under the same scope that differ
only in capitalization. Make sure that both of these follow the casing guide
(<a href="https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s5.3-camel-case">Google Java Style Guide §5.3</a>) and to be consistent if more
than one option is possible.</p>

<p>This checker will only find parameters that differ in capitalization with fields
that can be accessed from the parameter’s scope.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InconsistentCapitalization")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

</div>
</nav>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InconsistentHashCode<br>
            <small>Including fields in hashCode which are not compared in equals violates the contract of hashCode.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Implementations of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#hashCode</code> should not incorporate fields which the
implementation of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#equals</code> does not. This violates the contract of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code>: specifically, equal objects must have equal hashCodes.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">a</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">b</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="nd">@Override</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nd">@Nullable</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="o">((</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">a</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="nd">@Override</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="mi">31</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="n">first</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">10</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">20</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="n">second</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">10</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">40</span><span class="o">);</span>

<span class="n">first</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">second</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="c1">// true</span>
<span class="n">first</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="c1">// false</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The fix for this class is either to include a comparison of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">b</code> in the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">#equals</code>
method, or remove <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">b</code> from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">#hashCode</code>. The former is more likely to be correct.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InconsistentHashCode")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            IncorrectMainMethod<br>
            <small>'main' methods must be public, static, and void</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<h2 id="pre-java-25">Pre Java 25</h2>

<p>Prior to Java 25, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code> method must be <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code>, and return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void</code>
(see <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-12.html#jls-12.1.4">JLS §12.1.4</a>).</p>

<p>For example, the following method is confusing, because it is an overload of a
valid <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code> method (it has the same name and signature), but is not a valid
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code> method:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Test</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello world"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>$ java T.java
error: 'main' method is not declared 'public static'
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="java-25-and-later">Java 25 and later</h2>

<p>For Java 25 and later, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code> method must return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void</code> (see <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-12.html#jls-12.1.4">JLS §12.1.4</a>).
The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code> requirements have been dropped.</p>

<p>For example, the following method is confusing, because it is an overload of a
valid <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code> method (it has the same name and arguments), but does not return
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Test</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello world"</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>TIP: If you’re declaring a method that isn’t intended to be used as the main
method of your program, prefer to use a name other than <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">main</code>. It’s confusing
to humans and static analysis to see methods like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">private int main(String[]
args)</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IncorrectMainMethod")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InjectInvalidTargetingOnScopingAnnotation<br>
            <small>A scoping annotation's Target should include TYPE and METHOD.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Scope</code> annotations should be applicable to TYPE (annotating classes that
should be scoped) and to METHOD (annotating <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Provides</code> methods to apply scoping
to the returned object.</p>

<p>If an annotation’s use is restricted by <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Target</code> and it doesn’t include those
two element types, the annotation can’t be used where it should be able to be
used.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InjectInvalidTargetingOnScopingAnnotation")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InjectOnConstructorOfAbstractClass<br>
            <small>Constructors on abstract classes are never directly @Inject'ed, only the constructors of their subclasses can be @Inject'ed.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When dependency injection frameworks call constructors, they can only do so on
constructors of concrete classes, which can delegate to superclass constructors.
In the case of abstract classes, their constructors are only called by their
concrete subclasses, not directly by injection frameworks, so the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Inject</code>
annotation has no effect.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InjectOnConstructorOfAbstractClass")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

<div class="container">

          <h1>
            InjectScopeAnnotationOnInterfaceOrAbstractClass<br>
            <small>Scope annotation on an interface or abstract class is not allowed</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Scoping annotations are not inherited. They will have no effect if added to an
abstract type.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InjectScopeAnnotationOnInterfaceOrAbstractClass")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            InjectedConstructorAnnotations<br>
            <small>Injected constructors cannot be optional nor have binding annotations</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The constructor is annotated with @Inject(optional=true), or it is annotated
with @Inject and a binding annotation. This will cause a Guice runtime error.</p>

<p>For more information, see https://github.com/google/guice/wiki/InjectionPoints.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InjectedConstructorAnnotations")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InlineFormatString<br>
            <small>Prefer to create format strings inline, instead of extracting them to a single-use constant</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Prefer to use literal format strings directly in the call to a formatting method
over extracting them to a constant. That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">IllegalArgumentException</span><span class="o">(</span>
    <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">format</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Uh oh, can't use %s with %s"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgA</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgB</span><span class="o">));</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="no">ERROR_MESSAGE</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"Uh oh, can't use %s with %s"</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IllegalArgumentException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">format</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="no">ERROR_MESSAGE</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgA</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgB</span><span class="o">));</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Extracting the format string to a constant makes it harder to read the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String.format</code> call, and to see that the correct format arguments are being
passed.</p>

<p>If a single format string is used by multiple calls to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String.format</code>, consider
extracting a helper method instead of making the string a constant:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="nf">errorMessage</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">badArgA</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">badArgB</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">format</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"Uh oh, can't use %s with %s"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgA</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgB</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IllegalArgumentException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">errorMessage</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">badArgA</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">badArgB</span><span class="o">));</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InlineFormatString")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

            InlineMeSuggester<br>
            <small>This deprecated API looks inlineable. If you'd like the body of the API to be automatically inlined to its callers, please annotate it with @InlineMe. NOTE: the suggested fix makes the method final if it was not already.</small>
          </h1>

-->

          <h1>
            InlineTrivialConstant<br>
            <small>Consider inlining this constant</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Constants should be given names that emphasize the semantic meaning of the
value. If the name of the constant doesn’t convey any information that isn’t
clear from the value, consider inlining it.</p>

<p>For example, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">""</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="no">ONE</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="no">EMPTY_STRING</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">""</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="no">ONE</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="no">EMPTY_STRING</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InlineTrivialConstant")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            InputStreamSlowMultibyteRead<br>
            <small>Please also override int read(byte[], int, int), otherwise multi-byte reads from this input stream are likely to be slow.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Performance</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.io.InputStream</code> defines a single abstract method: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int read()</code>, which
subclasses implement to return bytes from the logical input stream.</p>

<p>However, in most circumstances, readers from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">InputStreams</code> use higher-level
methods like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">read(byte[], int offset, int length)</code> to read multiple bytes at a
time into a buffer. The default implementation of this method is to repeatedly
call <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">read()</code>. However, most InputStream implementations could do much better if
they can read multiple bytes at once (at the very least, avoiding unneeded
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">byte</code> -&gt; <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> -&gt; <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">byte</code> casts that are needed when implementing the read()
method over an underlying <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">byte</code> source).</p>

<p>The class in question implements <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int read()</code> without also overriding <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int
read(byte[], int, int)</code> and will thus be subject to the costs associated with
the default behavior of the multibyte read method.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InputStreamSlowMultibyteRead")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            IntFloatConversion<br>
            <small>Conversion from int to float may lose precision; use an explicit cast to float if this was intentional</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Implicit conversions from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">float</code> may lose precision when when calling
methods with overloads that accept both<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">float</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">double</code>.</p>

<p>For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Math.scalb</code> has overloads
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Math.html#scalb\(float,int\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Math.scalb(float, int)</code></a>
and
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Math.html#scalb\(double,int\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Math.scalb(double, int)</code></a>.</p>

<p>When passing an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> as the first argument, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Math.scalb(float, int)</code> will be
selected. If the result of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Math.scalb(float, int)</code> is then used as a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">double</code>,
this may result in a loss of precision.</p>

<p>To avoid this, an explicit cast to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">double</code> can be used to call the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Match.scalb(double, int)</code> overload:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">...</span>
<span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">y</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">...</span>
<span class="kt">double</span> <span class="n">f</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Math</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">scalb</span><span class="o">((</span><span class="kt">double</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IntFloatConversion")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            IntLongMath<br>
            <small>Expression of type int may overflow before being assigned to a long</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Performing an arithmetic expression on arguments of type int and then assigning
the result to a long is error-prone. The result is widened to a long as the
final step, and the intermediate results may overflow.</p>

<p>For example, the following expression exceeds <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer.MAX_VALUE</code> and overflows
to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-1857093632</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">nanosPerDay</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">24</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The corrected code (which has a value of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">86400000000000</code>) is:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">nanosPerDay</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">24L</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">60</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IntLongMath")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            InterruptedInCatchBlock<br>
            <small>Did you mean to call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() instead of Thread.interrupted()?</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>When attempting to fail-fast when interrupted, you should preserve the
interrupted status of the thread by calling
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Thread.currentThread().interrupt()</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">mightTimeOutOrBeCancelled</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="c1">// for example myFuture.get()</span>
<span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">InterruptedException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">Thread</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">currentThread</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">interrupt</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="c1">// Restore the interrupted status</span>
  <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">MyCheckedException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"[describe what task was interrupted]"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The current code is likely accidentally calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Thread.interrupted()</code>, which
clears the interrupt bit. (That is typically a no-op in this situation because
the interrupt bit is generally already unset when <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">InterruptedException</code> has
been thrown.) <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">thread.interrupt()</code> correctly restores the interrupt bit.</p>

<p>More information:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>https://web.archive.org/web/20201217182342/https://www.ibm.com/developerworks/java/library/j-jtp05236/index.html</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html#interrupt\(\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">thread.interrupt()</code></a></p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html#interrupted\(\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Thread.interrupted()</code></a></p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InterruptedInCatchBlock")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            InvalidLink<br>
            <small>This @link tag looks wrong.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This error is triggered by a Javadoc <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@link</code> tag that either is syntactically
invalid or can’t be resolved. See <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/tools/unix/javadoc.html#JSSOR654">javadoc documentation</a> for an
explanation of how to correctly format the contents of this tag.</p>

<h3 id="linking-to-generic-types">Linking to generic types</h3>

<p>Use the erased type of method parameters in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@link</code> tags. For example, write
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">{@link #foo(List)}</code> instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">{@link #foo(List&lt;Bah&gt;)}</code>. Javadoc does yet not
support generics in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@link</code> tags, due to a bug:
<a href="https://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-5096551">JDK-5096551</a>.</p>

<h3 id="limitations">Limitations</h3>

<p>This check is very limited in terms of which unresolved links it can be <em>sure</em>
are unresolvable. Code within Google is often compiled on a per-package or even
per-file basis, and Error Prone only has visibility into the current
compilation.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InvalidLink")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            IterableAndIterator<br>
            <small>Class should not implement both `Iterable` and `Iterator`</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>An <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator</code> is a <em>state-ful</em> instance that enables you to check whether it has
more elements (via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hasNext()</code>) and moves to the next one if any (via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">next()</code>),
while an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> is a representation of literally iterable elements. An
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> can generate multiple valid <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator</code>s, though.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IterableAndIterator")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            JUnit3FloatingPointComparisonWithoutDelta<br>
            <small>Floating-point comparison without error tolerance</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>JUnit 4’s floating-point overloads of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertEquals(expected, actual)</code> always
throw an exception, and some floating-point calls to JUnit 4’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertEquals</code> do
not even compile.</p>

<p>To continue comparing floating-point numbers using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Double.equals</code> semantics,
you may be able to cast one argument to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> or use Truth’s
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected)</code> /
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertWithMessage(message).that(actual).isEqualTo(expected)</code>.</p>

<p>Alternatively, you can switch to tolerance-based equality testing, which changes
your code’s behavior for negative zero (in JUnit and Truth) and for infinities
and NaN (in Truth). If you want that, use JUnit’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertEquals(expected,
actual, delta)</code> or Truth’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">isWithin(...).of(...)</code>, possibly with a tolerance of
zero.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JUnit3FloatingPointComparisonWithoutDelta")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

            JUnitAmbiguousTestClass<br>

        </div>

-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>For JUnit3-style tests, behavior is defined in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">junit.framework.TestCase</code> and
tests add behavior by overriding methods. For JUnit4-style tests, special
behavior happens with fields and methods annotated with JUnit 4 annotations.
Having JUnit4-style tests extend from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">junit.framework.TestCase</code> (directly or
indirectly) historically has been a source of test bugs and unexpected behavior
(e.g.: teardown logic and/or verification does not run because JUnit doesn’t
call the inherited code).</p>

<p>Error Prone also cannot infer whether the test class runs with JUnit 3 or JUnit
4.</p>

<p>Thus, even if the test class runs with JUnit 4, Error Prone will not run
additional checks which can catch common errors with JUnit 4 test classes.
Either use only JUnit4 classes and annotations and remove the inheritance from
TestCase, or use only JUnit 3 and remove the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Test</code> annotations. When looking
for replacements for base test classes, consider using Rules (see the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Rule</code>
annotation and implementations of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TestRule</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">MethodRule</code>).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JUnitAmbiguousTestClass")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>
    <footer class="footer">
<div class="container">
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col-lg-12">
      <p class="text-muted">&copy; 2026 Google</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
</footer>

            <small>duration.getNano() only accesses the underlying nanosecond adjustment from the whole second.</small>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>If you call duration.getNano(), you must also call duration.getSeconds() in ‘nearby’ code. If you are trying to convert this duration to nanoseconds, you probably meant to use duration.toNanos() instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaDurationGetSecondsGetNano")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>

            JavaDurationWithNanos<br>
            <small>Use of java.time.Duration.withNanos(int) is not allowed.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>

          </dl>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Duration’s withNanos(int) method is often a source of bugs because it returns a copy of the current Duration instance, but <em>only</em> the nano field is mutated (the seconds field is copied directly). Use Duration.ofSeconds(duration.getSeconds(), nanos) instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaDurationWithNanos")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            JavaInstantGetSecondsGetNano<br>
            <small>instant.getNano() only accesses the underlying nanosecond adjustment from the whole second.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>If you call instant.getNano(), you must also call instant.getEpochSecond() in ‘nearby’ code. If you are trying to convert this instant to nanoseconds, you probably meant to use Instants.toEpochNanos(instant) instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaInstantGetSecondsGetNano")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

            JavaTimeDefaultTimeZone<br>
            <small>java.time APIs that silently use the default system time-zone are not allowed.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using APIs that silently use the default system time-zone is dangerous. The default system time-zone can vary from machine to machine or JVM to JVM. You must choose an explicit ZoneId.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaTimeDefaultTimeZone")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            JavaUtilDate<br>
            <small>Date has a bad API that leads to bugs; prefer java.time.Instant or LocalDate.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Date</code> API is full of
<a href="https://codeblog.jonskeet.uk/2017/04/23/all-about-java-util-date/">major design flaws and pitfalls</a>
and should be avoided at all costs. Prefer the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time</code> APIs, specifically,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time.Instant</code> (for physical time) and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time.LocalDate[Time]</code> (for
civil time).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaUtilDate")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

            JavaxInjectOnFinalField<br>
            <small>@javax.inject.Inject cannot be put on a final field.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>According to the JSR-330 spec, the @javax.inject.Inject annotation cannot go on
final fields.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("JavaxInjectOnFinalField")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>
