    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ModifyCollectionInEnhancedForLoop<br>
            <small>Modifying a collection while iterating over it in a loop may cause a ConcurrentModificationException to be thrown or lead to undefined behavior.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>From the javadoc for
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/java/util/Iterator.html#remove--"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator.remove</code></a>:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>The behavior of an iterator is unspecified if the underlying collection is
modified while the iteration is in progress in any way other than by calling
this method, unless an overriding class has specified a concurrent
modification policy.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Iterator</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">it</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">ids</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">iterator</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">it</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasNext</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">shouldRemove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">it</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">next</span><span class="o">()))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">it</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">remove</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">ids</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">shouldRemove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">id</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">ids</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">remove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">id</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// will cause a ConcurrentModificationException!</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>TIP: This pattern is simpler with Java 8’s
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/Collection.html#removeIf-java.util.function.Predicate-"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection.removeIf</code></a>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">ids</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">removeIf</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">shouldRemove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">id</span><span class="o">));</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ModifyCollectionInEnhancedForLoop")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ModifySourceCollectionInStream<br>
            <small>Modifying the backing source during stream operations may cause unintended results.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>From the javadoc for
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/util/stream/package-summary.html#NonInterference"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.stream: Non-interference</code></a>:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Accordingly, behavioral parameters in stream pipelines whose source might not
be concurrent should never modify the stream’s data source. A behavioral
parameter is said to interfere with a non-concurrent data source if it
modifies, or causes to be modified, the stream’s data source. The need for
non-interference applies to all pipelines, not just parallel ones. Unless the
stream source is concurrent, modifying a stream’s data source during execution
hg of a stream pipeline can cause exceptions, incorrect answers, or
nonconformant behavior.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">mutableValues</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">stream</span><span class="o">()</span>
  <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">filter</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">5</span><span class="o">)</span>
  <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">collect</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Collectors</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">toList</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="c1">// Terminate stream before source modification.</span>
  <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">forEach</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nl">mutableValues:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">remove</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">mutableValues</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">stream</span><span class="o">()</span>
  <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">filter</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">5</span><span class="o">)</span>
  <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">forEach</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nl">mutableValues:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">remove</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ModifySourceCollectionInStream")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            MultipleUnaryOperatorsInMethodCall<br>
            <small>Avoid having multiple unary operators acting on the same variable in a method call</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Increment operators in method calls are dubious and while argument lists are
evaluated left-to-right, documentation suggests that code not rely on this
specification. In addition, code is clearer when each expression contains at
most one side effect.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("MultipleUnaryOperatorsInMethodCall")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            MutablePublicArray<br>
            <small>Non-empty arrays are mutable, so this `public static final` array is not a constant and can be modified by clients of this class.  Prefer an ImmutableList, or provide an accessor method that returns a defensive copy.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Nonzero-length arrays are mutable. Declaring one <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public static final</code> indicates
that the developer expects it to be a constant, which is not the case. Making it
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public</code> is especially dangerous since clients of this code can modify the
contents of the array.</p>

<p>There are two ways to fix this problem:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Refactor the array to an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code>.</li>
  <li>Make the array <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">private</code> and add a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public</code> method that returns a copy of
the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">private</code> array.</li>
</ol>

<p>See <a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=BIpDDwAAQBAJ">Effective Java 3rd Edition §15</a> for more details.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("MutablePublicArray")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            NamedLikeContextualKeyword<br>
            <small>Avoid naming of classes and methods that is similar to contextual keywords.  When invoking such a method, qualify it.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The problem we’re trying to prevent is clashes between the names of
classes/methods and contextual keywords. Clashes can occur when (1.) naming a
class/method, or (2.) when invoking.</p>

<h1 id="when-naming">When naming</h1>

<p>Change problematic names for classes and methods.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="c1">// This can clash with the contextual keyword "yield"</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">yield</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Another example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// This can clash with Java modules (JPMS)</span>
<span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">module</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="o">...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h1 id="when-invoking">When invoking</h1>

<p>In recent versions of Java, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">yield</code> is a restricted identifier:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">T</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">yield</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
  <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">yield</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>$ javac --release 20 T.java
T.java:3: error: invalid use of a restricted identifier 'yield'
    yield();
    ^
  (to invoke a method called yield, qualify the yield with a receiver or type name)
1 error
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To invoke existing methods called <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">yield</code>, use qualified names:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">T</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">yield</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
  <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">yield</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">T</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">yield</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
  <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="no">T</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">yield</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">T</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">yield</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
  <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">I</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="no">T</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">yield</span><span class="o">();</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NamedLikeContextualKeyword")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            NarrowCalculation<br>
            <small>This calculation may lose precision compared to its target type.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Integer division is suspicious when the target type of the expression is a
float. For example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">double</span> <span class="no">ONE_HALF</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span> <span class="o">/</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="c1">// Actually 0.</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If you specifically want the integer result, consider pulling out variable to
make it clear what’s happening. For example, instead of:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// Deduct 10% from the grade for every week the assignment is late:</span>
<span class="kt">float</span> <span class="n">adjustedGrade</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">grade</span> <span class="o">-</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">days</span> <span class="o">/</span> <span class="mi">7</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="o">.</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Prefer:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// Deduct 10% from the grade for every week the assignment is late:</span>
<span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">fullWeeks</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">days</span> <span class="o">/</span> <span class="mi">7</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kt">float</span> <span class="n">adjustedGrade</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">grade</span> <span class="o">-</span> <span class="n">fullWeeks</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="o">.</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Similarly, multiplication of two <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> values which are then cast to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long</code> is
problematic, as the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> multiplication could overflow. It’s better to perform
the multiplication using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long</code> arithmetic.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="nf">secondsToNanos</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">seconds</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">seconds</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1_000_000_000</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="c1">// Oops; starts overflowing around 2.15 seconds.</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Instead, prefer:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="nf">secondsToNanos</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">seconds</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">seconds</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1_000_000_000L</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="c1">// Or ((long) seconds) * 1_000_000_000.</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NarrowCalculation")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

    <div class="container">

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            NarrowingCompoundAssignment<br>
            <small>Compound assignments may hide dangerous casts</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The compound assignment <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E1 op= E2</code> could be mistaken for being equivalent to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E1 = E1 op E2</code>. However, this is not the case: compound assignment operators
automatically cast the result of the computation to the type on the left hand
side. So <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E1 op= E2</code> is actually equivalent to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E1 = (T) (E1 op E2)</code>, where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">T</code>
is the type of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">E1</code>.</p>

<p>If the type of the expression is wider than the type of the variable (i.e. the
variable is a byte, char, short, or float), then the compound assignment will
perform a narrowing primitive conversion. Attempting to perform the equivalent
simple assignment would generate a compilation error.</p>

<p>For example, the following does not compile:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">byte</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">&lt;&lt;</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="c1">//    ^</span>
<span class="c1">// error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from int to byte</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>However, the compound assignment form is allowed:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">byte</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">&lt;&lt;=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Similarly, if the expression is a floating point type (float or double), and the
variable is an integral type (long, int, short, byte, or char), then an implicit
conversion will be performed.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">l</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">180</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="n">l</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">l</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mf">2.0f</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="c1">//    ^</span>
<span class="c1">// error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from float to long</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Again, the compound assignment form is permitted:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">l</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">180</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="n">l</span> <span class="o">*=</span> <span class="mf">2.0f</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>See Puzzle #9 in ‘Java Puzzlers: Traps, Pitfalls, and Corner Cases’ for more
information.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NarrowingCompoundAssignment")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            NewFileSystem<br>
            <small>Starting in JDK 13, this call is ambiguous with FileSystem.newFileSystem(Path,Map)</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Starting in JDK 13, calls to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FileSystem.newFileSystem(path, null)</code> are
ambiguous.</p>

<p>The calls match both:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/13/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/file/FileSystems.html#newFileSystem\(java.nio.file.Path,java.lang.ClassLoader\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FileSystem.newFileSystem(Path, ClassLoader)</code></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/13/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/file/FileSystems.html#newFileSystem\(java.nio.file.Path,java.util.Map\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FileSystem.newFileSystem(Path, Map&lt;?, ?&gt;)</code></a></li>
</ul>

<p>To disambiguate, add a cast to the desired type, to preserve the pre-JDK 13
behaviour.</p>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">FileSystem</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newFileSystem</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ClassLoader</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Instead of this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">FileSystem</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newFileSystem</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NewFileSystem")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            NonApiType<br>
            <small>Certain types should not be passed across API boundaries.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Flags instances of non-API types from being accepted or returned in public APIs.</p>

<h3 id="what-it-flags">What it flags</h3>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Primitive Arrays:</strong> Methods accepting or returning primitive or
boxed-primitive arrays (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int[]</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Integer[]</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">double[]</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Double[]</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long[]</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Long[]</code>). Prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableIntArray</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableDoubleArray</code>, or
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableLongArray</code> instead.
    <ul>
      <li><em>Note:</em> Var-args parameters (e.g. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int... rest</code>) are <strong>not</strong> flagged, as
var-args is idiomatic Java for parameter lists.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li><strong>Collection Implementations:</strong> Accepting or returning concrete collection
classes (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ArrayList</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">LinkedList</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">HashSet</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">LinkedHashSet</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TreeSet</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">HashMap</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">LinkedHashMap</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TreeMap</code>). Prefer interface types (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code>).</li>
  <li><strong>Immutable Collections as Parameters:</strong> Accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableCollection</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code>, or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableMap</code> as method parameters.
Prefer accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map</code>, or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> for
parameter generality.</li>
  <li><strong>Optional Parameters:</strong> Accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Optional</code> or
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.common.base.Optional</code> as method parameters. Prefer method
overloading: creating one signature with the parameter and one without (or
use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code> parameters).</li>
  <li><strong><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.common.base.Pair</code>:</strong> Passing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pair</code> across API boundaries.
Define a well-named class or record instead.</li>
  <li><strong>Iterators &amp; Streams:</strong> Returning <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator</code> (prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code> or collecting
to an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code>/<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code>) or accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code> as a parameter
(prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection</code>).
    <ul>
      <li>Returning stateful single-use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator</code>s limits caller options</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li><strong>ProtoTime Types:</strong> Using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.protobuf.Duration</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Timestamp</code>, or
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.type.*</code> types across public APIs instead of standard
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.time.*</code> types (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Duration</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Instant</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">LocalDate</code>, etc.).</li>
  <li><strong>Flogger Loggers:</strong> Passing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FluentLogger</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">GoogleLogger</code> instances
across method boundaries; this can break standard per-class logger
initialization patterns.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="why">Why</h3>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Type Generality &amp; Interface Abstraction:</strong> Methods should accept abstract
interface types (e.g., <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code> rather than <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ArrayList</code>) to give callers
flexibility in implementation details.</li>
  <li><strong>Immutability &amp; Safety:</strong> Primitive arrays are mutable and expose internal
array state directly to callers. Guava’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableIntArray</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableDoubleArray</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableLongArray</code> provide immutable, safe,
and efficient alternatives.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NonApiType")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            NonAtomicVolatileUpdate<br>
            <small>This update of a volatile variable is non-atomic</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The volatile modifier ensures that updates to a variable are propagated
predictably to other threads. A read of a volatile variable always returns the
most recent write by any thread.</p>

<p>However, this does not mean that all updates to a volatile variable are atomic.
For example, if you increment or decrement a volatile variable, you are actually
doing (1) a read of the variable, (2) an increment or decrement of a local copy,
and (3) a write back to the variable. Each step is atomic individually, but the
whole sequence is not, and it will cause a race condition if two threads try to
increment or decrement a volatile variable at the same time. The same is true
for compound assignment, e.g. foo += bar.</p>

<p>If you intended for this update to be atomic, you should wrap all update
operations on this variable in a synchronized block. If the variable is an
integer, you could use an AtomicInteger instead of a volatile int.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NonAtomicVolatileUpdate")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            NonCanonicalType<br>
            <small>This type is referred to by a non-canonical name, which may be misleading.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Types being referred to by non-canonical names can be confusing. For example,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Entries</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">ImmutableMap</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Entry</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="o">&gt;&gt;</span> <span class="n">entries</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nf">Entries</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">map</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">entries</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">copyOf</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">entrySet</span><span class="o">());</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>There is nothing special about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableMap.Entry</code>; it is precisely the same
type as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Map.Entry</code>. This example makes it look deceptively as though
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList&lt;ImmutableMap.Entry&lt;?, ?&gt;&gt;</code> is an immutable type and therefore
safe to store indefinitely, when really it offers no more safety than
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList&lt;Map.Entry&lt;?, ?&gt;&gt;</code>. You should use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList&lt;Map.Entry&lt;?,
?&gt;&gt;</code> instead, so it’s obvious what type you’re referring to.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NonCanonicalType")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            NonOverridingEquals<br>
            <small>equals method doesn't override Object.equals</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Defining a method that looks like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#equals</code> but doesn’t actually override
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#equals</code> is dangerous. The result of the comparison could differ
depending on the declared type of the argument passed into the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> call.</p>

<p>For example, consider this code:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Example</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">value</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nf">Example</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">value</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">value</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">value</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Example</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">value</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="n">other</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">value</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Example</span> <span class="n">exampleA</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Example</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="nc">Example</span> <span class="n">exampleB</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Example</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">out</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">exampleA</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">exampleB</span><span class="o">));</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This will print <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">true</code>. Suppose you refactor it so that the variable <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">exampleB</code>
is declared as an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> instead. Now this code will print <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">false</code>, because
Java’s overload resolution will choose the default <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals(Object)</code>
implementation instead of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals(Example)</code> method defined in this class.</p>

<p>If this equals method is intended to be a type-specific helper for an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code>
method that <em>does</em> override <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#equals</code>, either inline it into the
overriding <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> method or rename it to something other than <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> to
avoid ambiguity in overload resolution.</p>

<p>If you don’t want to write and maintain <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> methods by hand,
consider rewriting this class to use
<a href="https://github.com/google/auto/tree/master/value">AutoValue</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NonOverridingEquals")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            NullOptional<br>
            <small>Passing a literal null to an Optional parameter is almost certainly a mistake. Did you mean to provide an empty Optional?</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Passing a literal <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> to an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code> accepting parameter is likely a bug.
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code> is already designed to encode missing values through a non-<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>
instance.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">double</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">i</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">i</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">doubled</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kt">double</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">doubled</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kt">double</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">empty</span><span class="o">());</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This is a scenario that can easily happen when refactoring code from accepting
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code> parameters to accept <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code>s. Note that the check will not match
if the parameter is explicitly annotated <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullOptional")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            NullableConstructor<br>
            <small>Constructors should not be annotated with @Nullable since they cannot return null</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Style</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Constructors never return null.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullableConstructor")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            NullableOptional<br>
            <small>Using an Optional variable which is expected to possibly be null is discouraged. It is best to indicate the absence of the value by assigning it an empty optional.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code> is a container object which may or may not contain a value. The
presence or absence of the contained value should be demonstrated by the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code> object itself.</p>

<p>Using an Optional variable which is expected to possibly be null is discouraged.
An nullable Optional which uses <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> to indicate the absence of the value will
lead to extra work for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> checking when using the object and even cause
exceptions such as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NullPointerException</code>. It is best to indicate the absence of
the value by assigning it an empty optional.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullableOptional")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            NullablePrimitiveArray<br>
            <small>@Nullable type annotations should not be used for primitive types since they cannot be null</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Style</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>For <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable</code> type annotations (such as
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">org.checkerframework.checker.nullness.qual.Nullable</code>), <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable byte[]</code> means
a ‘non-null array of nullable bytes’, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">byte @Nullable []</code> means a ‘nullable
array of non-null bytes’. Since primitive types cannot be null, the former is
incorrect.</p>

<p>Some other nullness annotations (such as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.annotation.Nullable</code>) are
<em>declaration</em> annotations rather than <em>type</em> annotations. Their meaning is
different: For such annotations, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Nullable byte[]</code> refers to ‘a nullable array
of non-null bytes,’ and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">byte @Nullable []</code> is rejected by javac. Thus, this
check never reports errors for usages of declaration annotations.</p>

<p>See also: https://checkerframework.org/manual/#faq-array-syntax-meaning</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullablePrimitiveArray")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            NullableTypeParameter<br>
            <small>Nullness annotations directly on type parameters are interpreted differently by different tools</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Nullness annotations directly on type parameters are interpreted differently by
different tools.
— unless you are using the Checker Framework.</p>

<h3 id="tool-interpretations-and-suggested-alternatives">Tool interpretations and suggested alternatives</h3>

<h4 id="class-foonullable-t"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo&lt;@Nullable T&gt;</code></h4>

<p>To the Checker Framework, this means that a given type argument <em>must</em> be
nullable. For example, in the Checker Framework’s default JDK stubs,
<a href="https://github.com/typetools/jdk/blob/1973fa0811588dd0bb025fdc99345cdb887b3b52/src/java.base/share/classes/java/lang/ThreadLocal.java#L84-L91">the type argument to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code> must be nullable</a>.</p>

<p>To Kotlin, this means that the type argument <em>can</em> be nullable but need not be
so.</p>

<p>If you want the Checker Framework interpretation, then keep your code as it is,
and suppress this warning. If you want the “<em>can</em> be nullable” interpretation,
change to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo&lt;T extends @Nullable Object&gt;</code>.</p>

<p>The effects of that change would be:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>It is a behavior change for the Checker Framework, one that could even
produce local or non-local the Checker Framework failures. As discussed
above, it may be a desirable change, and it’s likely to be safe unless you
are using it with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code>.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>This is probably not a behavior change for Kotlin.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h4 id="class-foononnull-t"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo&lt;@NonNull T&gt;</code></h4>

<p>To the Checker Framework, this means to allow <em>any</em> nullness for the type
argument(!). (It
<a href="https://checkerframework.org/manual/#generics-bounds-syntax">sets the <em>lower</em> bound</a>
to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@NonNull</code>, which is already the default there.)</p>

<p>To Kotlin, this means that the type argument must be non-nullable.</p>

<p>Users probably want <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo&lt;T extends @NonNull Object&gt;</code>. Or, if they’re
within the scope of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@NullMarked</code> and they are using tools that recognize it
(such as Kotlin), they may prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo&lt;T&gt;</code>, which is equivalent but
shorter.</p>

<p>The effects of that change would be:</p>

<ul>
  <li>It is a behavior change for the Checker Framework, one that could produce
local or non-local the Checker Framework failures. But it’s likely to be a
desirable change.</li>
  <li>It is probably not a behavior change for Kotlin.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="jspecify-specification">JSpecify specification</h3>

<p>The JSpecify spec says that usages of their annotations on type parameters are
unrecognized
(<a href="https://jspecify.dev/docs/api/org/jspecify/annotations/Nullable.html#applicability">Javadoc</a>,
<a href="https://jspecify.dev/docs/spec/#recognized-locations-for-type-use-annotations">spec</a>).
This specification choice is motivated by the disagreement in tool behavior
discussed above.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullableTypeParameter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            NullableWildcard<br>
            <small>Nullness annotations directly on wildcard types are interpreted differently by different tools</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Nullness annotations directly on wildcard types are interpreted differently by
different tools.
— unless you are using the Checker Framework.</p>

<h3 id="tool-interpretations-and-suggested-alternatives">Tool interpretations and suggested alternatives</h3>

<h4 id="foonullable-"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;@Nullable ?&gt;</code></h4>

<p>To the Checker Framework, this means that the type argument <em>must</em> be nullable.
They use this
<a href="https://github.com/typetools/jdk/blob/1973fa0811588dd0bb025fdc99345cdb887b3b52/src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.java#L269">in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ExecutorService</code></a>.</p>

<p>To Kotlin, this <a href="https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/KT-40498/Nullability-annotations-on-Java-wildcard-itself">has no effect</a>. That means that the type argument
<em>can</em> be nullable but need not be so.</p>

<p>While Checker Framework users do sometimes want <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;@Nullable ?&gt;</code>, we commonly
see them use it in places where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;?&gt;</code> would also be correct and would be more
flexible. To fully preserve Kotlin behavior, Kotlin users may wish to write
“<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;? extends @Nullable Object&gt;</code>” (unless they are within the scope of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@NullMarked</code>, in which case <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;?&gt;</code> is equivalent).</p>

<p>The effects of that change would be:</p>

<ul>
  <li>It is a behavior change for the Checker Framework, one that could produce
local or non-local the Checker Framework failures. But it’s likely to be a
desirable change except in the context of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ExecutorService</code> and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Future</code>
objects that it produces.</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;?&gt;</code> is probably not a behavior change for Kotlin.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="foononnull-"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;@NonNull ?&gt;</code></h4>

<p>To the Checker Framework, this means that the type argument must be
non-nullable. (See
<a href="https://checkerframework.org/manual/#annotations-on-wildcards">the Checker Framework docs</a>.)</p>

<p>To Kotlin, this <a href="https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/KT-40498/Nullability-annotations-on-Java-wildcard-itself">has no effect</a>. That means that the type argument can
still be nullable.</p>

<p>We recommend a change to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;? extends @NonNull Object&gt;</code> (or, within the scope
of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@NullMarked</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo&lt;? extends Object&gt;</code>).</p>

<p>The effects of that change would be:</p>

<ul>
  <li>It is a no-op for the Checker Framework.</li>
  <li>It could produce errors for Kotlin users. But these errors are likely to be
what was intended all along.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="jspecify-specification">JSpecify specification</h3>

<p>The JSpecify spec says that usages of their annotations on wildcard types are
unrecognized
(<a href="https://jspecify.dev/docs/api/org/jspecify/annotations/Nullable.html#applicability">Javadoc</a>,
<a href="https://jspecify.dev/docs/spec/#recognized-locations-for-type-use-annotations">spec</a>).
This specification choice is motivated by the disagreement in tool behavior
discussed above.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NullableWildcard")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ObjectToString<br>
            <small>Calling toString on Objects that don't override toString() doesn't provide useful information</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">toString</code> on objects that don’t override <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">toString()</code> doesn’t provide
useful information (just the class name and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code>).</p>

<p>Consider overriding toString() function to return a meaningful String describing
the object.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ObjectToString")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ObjectsHashCodePrimitive<br>
            <small>Objects.hashCode(Object o) should not be passed a primitive value</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Objects.hashCode</code> takes an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code> parameter, and will either return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code> when
the parameter is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>, or call the underlying <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> function of the
Object reference.</p>

<p>Passing a primitive value to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Objects.hashCode</code> function results in boxing the
primitive, then calling the boxed object’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code>. You can get the same
result by using, e.g.: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Long.hashCode(long)</code> to get the effective hash code of a
primitive <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">long</code>. If you’re calling this method outside of your own <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code>
implementation, prefer to use the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">BoxedClass.hashCode(primitive)</code> functions to
avoid unwanted boxed.</p>

<p>If you’re implementing a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> function for your <strong>own</strong> class that
consists of a single primitive value, you may want to consider some of these
alternatives:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// This function will box intValue into an Integer, and wrap *that* in an</span>
  <span class="c1">// array, but will generate a hashCode which is likely to be different than</span>
  <span class="c1">// the hashCode of the boxed version of the intValue. This makes it easier</span>
  <span class="c1">// to add more fields to the class and hashCode method (just by adding more</span>
  <span class="c1">// fields to the hash call), but comes at a potential performance penalty.</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">Objects</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hash</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">intValue</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// This function will avoid boxing the int to an Integer, and is an explicit</span>
  <span class="c1">// acknowledgement that the hashCode() of *this* class is the same as the</span>
  <span class="c1">// hash code of the underlying intValue.</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hashCode</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">intValue</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ObjectsHashCodePrimitive")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            OperatorPrecedence<br>
            <small>Use grouping parenthesis to make the operator precedence explicit</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Style</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <a href="https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s4.7-grouping-parentheses">Google Java Style Guide §4.7</a> states:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Optional grouping parentheses are omitted only when author and reviewer agree
that there is no reasonable chance the code will be misinterpreted without
them, nor would they have made the code easier to read. It is not reasonable
to assume that every reader has the entire Java operator precedence table
memorized.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Use grouping parentheses to disambiguate expressions that could be
misinterpreted.</p>

<p>For example, consider this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">d</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="n">c</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">e</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">c</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">d</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">z</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">&lt;&lt;</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Instead of this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">r</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="n">c</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">e</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">c</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">d</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">z</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="n">y</span> <span class="o">&lt;&lt;</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OperatorPrecedence")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            OptionalMapToOptional<br>
            <small>Mapping to another Optional will yield a nested Optional. Did you mean flatMap?</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional#map</code> (or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional#transform</code>) to map to another <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code>
might indicate an error, or at least quite hard-to-reason-about code that may
turn into an error.</p>

<p>For example,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">AccountManager</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="cm">/** Retrieves the current user, or absent if not logged in. */</span>
  <span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Account</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">getUser</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="cm">/**
   * Returns an administrative token for the user, or absent if they do not have
   * such privileges.
   */</span>
  <span class="nc">Optional</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Token</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">getAdminToken</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doScaryAdminThings</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">getUser</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nl">AccountManager:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">getAdminToken</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">isPresent</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="c1">// do privileged things.</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>In this case, assuming <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getAdminToken</code> does not throw, the conditional is
equivalent to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getUser().isPresent()</code>, which is not what was intended.
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">getUser().flatMap(AccountManager::getAdminToken).isPresent()</code> would be correct.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OptionalMapToOptional")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            OptionalNotPresent<br>
            <small>This Optional has been confirmed to be empty at this point, so the call to `get()` or `orElseThrow()` will always throw.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">get()</code> on an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional</code> that is not present will result in a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NoSuchElementException</code>.</p>

<p>This check detects cases where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">get()</code> is called when the optional is definitely
not present, e.g.:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">isPresent</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="c1">// this will throw a NoSuchElementException</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">isEmpty</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="c1">// this will throw a NoSuchElementException</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>These cases are almost definitely bugs; the intent may have been to invert the
test:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">isPresent</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OptionalNotPresent")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            OrphanedFormatString<br>
            <small>String literal contains format specifiers, but is not passed to a format method</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Passing a string that contains format specifiers to a method that does not
perform string formatting is usually a mistake.</p>

<p>Do this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">isValid</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">arg</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IllegalArgumentException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">format</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"invalid arg: %s"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">arg</span><span class="o">));</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>or this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">logger</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">atWarning</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">log</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"invalid arg: %s"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">arg</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Not this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">isValid</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">arg</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IllegalArgumentException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"invalid arg: %s"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>or this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">logger</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">atWarning</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">log</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"invalid arg: %s"</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If the method you’re calling actually accepts a format string, you can annotate
that method with <a href="https://errorprone.info/api/latest/com/google/errorprone/annotations/FormatMethod.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@FormatMethod</code></a> to ensure that callers correctly pass
format strings (and to inform Error Prone that the method call you’re making
doesn’t orphan a format string).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OrphanedFormatString")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            OutlineNone<br>
            <small>Setting CSS outline style to none or 0 (while not otherwise providing visual focus indicators) is inaccessible for users navigating a web page without a mouse.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">outline</code> CSS property provides visual indicators as to which element is
currently selected within a web page. These are the dotted lines you see
surrounding links, etc. when you tab to them using the keyboard.</p>

<p><img src="https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/gh-pages/images/Outline%20Demonstration.png" alt="A link shown with and without a focus outline." /></p>

<p>These indicators are important for users navigating without a mouse (such as
those with visual or mobility impairments). Setting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">outline</code> style to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"none"</code>
or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code> removes these indicators, leaving these users without any way to tell
where they are within the page, therefore making the page inaccessible.</p>

<p>Caveat: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">outline</code> is not the <em>only</em> way to emphasize selected elements. You may
instead choose to change the background color, add an underline, or otherwise
make them visually distinct. Learn more &amp; get alternative suggestions at
<a href="https://outlinenone.com">OutlineNone.com</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OutlineNone")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            OverrideThrowableToString<br>
            <small>To return a custom message with a Throwable class, one should override getMessage() instead of toString().</small>
          </h1>
        </div>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
