        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            Overrides<br>
            <small>Varargs doesn't agree for overridden method</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: overrides</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Even though varargs methods are different than methods with an array parameter
as the last parameter, varargs methods are compiled into bytecode as methods
with an array as the last parameter. When a varargs method is <em>called</em>, the Java
compiler will insert instructions to automatically box the varargs arguments
into an array.</p>

<p>This detail means that, for example, you can’t declare two methods in the same
class where the final parameter is an array in one method, and a varargs of the
same type in the other:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">bah</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">double</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">double</span><span class="o">...</span> <span class="n">others</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">bah</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">double</span> <span class="n">baz</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">double</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">myArray</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span> <span class="c1">// ERROR: bah(double, double[]) already defined</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This also means that one method with varargs can override another method with an
array as the final parameter:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">A</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span><span class="o">...</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">B</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="no">A</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@Override</span>
  <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This overriding may be unintentional (since the signatures ‘look’ different, the
programmer may be unaware that an overriding has occurred).</p>

<p>Even if this overriding is intentional, it causes inconsistencies at call-sites,
as the code required to invoke the overridden method depends on the static type
of the variable being operated on.</p>

<p>Given the example classes above, observe the result on the client side:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Client</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="no">B</span> <span class="n">b</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="no">B</span><span class="o">();</span>
    <span class="no">A</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">;</span>

    <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">new</span> <span class="kt">int</span><span class="o">[]{</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">});</span> <span class="c1">// OK, array invocation of varargs method</span>
    <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">new</span> <span class="kt">int</span><span class="o">[]{</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">});</span> <span class="c1">// OK, direct array invocation</span>

    <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// OK, varargs invocation with 1 element</span>

    <span class="c1">// Very strange compile-time error:</span>
    <span class="c1">// error: A.something(int...) is defined in an inaccessible class or interface</span>
    <span class="n">b</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">something</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To avoid these ambiguities, use the same parameter style (varargs or explicit
arrays) when overriding methods.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("Overrides")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            OverridesGuiceInjectableMethod<br>
            <small>This method is not annotated with @Inject, but it overrides a method that is annotated with @com.google.inject.Inject. Guice will inject this method, and it is recommended to annotate it explicitly.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Unlike with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@javax.inject.Inject</code>, if a method overrides a method annotated
with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@com.google.inject.Inject</code>, Guice will inject it even if it itself is not
annotated. This differs from the behavior of methods that override
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@javax.inject.Inject</code> methods since according to the JSR-330 spec, a method
that overrides a method annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@javax.inject.Inject</code> will not be
injected unless it itself is annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Inject</code>. Because of this
difference, it is recommended that you annotate this method explicitly.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OverridesGuiceInjectableMethod")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            OverridingMethodInconsistentArgumentNamesChecker<br>
            <small>Arguments of overriding method are inconsistent with overridden method.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Inconsistently ordered parameters in method overrides mostly indicate an
accidental bug in the overriding method. An example for an overriding method
with inconsistent parameter names:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">A</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">foo</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">baz</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">B</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="no">A</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@Override</span>
  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">foo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">baz</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("OverridingMethodInconsistentArgumentNamesChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ParameterName<br>
            <small>Detects `/* name= */`-style comments on actual parameters where the name doesn't match the formal parameter</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>In certain contexts literal arguments - such as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">0</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">""</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">true</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">false</code>,
or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> - can make it difficult for readers to know what a method will do.
Defining methods that take boolean parameters or otherwise expect users to pass
in ambiguous literals is generally discouraged. However, when you must call such
a method you’re encouraged to use the parameter name as an inline comment at the
call site, so that readers don’t need to look at the method declaration to
understand the parameter’s purpose.</p>

<p>Error Prone recognizes such comments that use the following formatting, and
emits an error if the comment doesn’t match the name of the corresponding formal
parameter:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">booleanMethod</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="cm">/* enableFoo= */</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Varargs methods are also supported using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">...</code> syntax: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void varargsMethod(/*
states...= */ true, true, false);</code></p>

<p>The check also recognizes comments with whitespace variations, e.g. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">/*foo =*/</code>,
but the form <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">/* foo= */</code> is preferred.</p>

<p>If the comment deliberately does not match the formal parameter name, using a
regular block comment without the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">=</code> is recommended: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">/* enableFoo */</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ParameterName")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            PatternMatchingInstanceof<br>
            <small>This code can be simplified to use a pattern-matching instanceof.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Pattern matching with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceof</code> allows writing this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">handle</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nf">Point</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">handlePoint</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">else</span> <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">handleString</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">s</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>which is more concise than an instanceof and a separate cast:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">handle</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Point</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Point</span> <span class="n">point</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Point</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="n">handlePoint</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">point</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">x</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="n">point</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">y</span><span class="o">());</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">else</span> <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">o</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">o</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="n">handleString</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">s</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>For more information on pattern matching and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceof</code>, see
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/language/pattern-matching-instanceof.html">Pattern Matching for the instanceof Operator</a></p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("PatternMatchingInstanceof")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            PreferCharsetOverload<br>
            <small>Prefer calling overloads that accept a Charset over those that accept a String encoding name.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<h1 id="prefercharsetoverload">PreferCharsetOverload</h1>

<p>APIs that accept a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code> charset name often have an overload that accepts a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.nio.charset.Charset</code>. Prefer using the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Charset</code> overload, as it provides
stronger typing.</p>

<p>If a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Charset</code> instance is being converted to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code> (e.g. via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.name()</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.displayName()</code>, or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.toString()</code>) just to call the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code> overload, the
conversion can simply be removed.</p>

<p><strong>Note:</strong> This check relies on method parameter name information being preserved
in class files at runtime. Therefore, compiling the targeted libraries or JDK
stubs with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-parameters</code> flag (introduced in
<a href="https://openjdk.org/jeps/118">JEP 118</a>) is required for the check to discover
candidate parameters reliably.</p>

<h2 id="examples">Examples</h2>

<h3 id="instead-of-this">Instead of this…</h3>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">OutputStreamWriter</span> <span class="n">writer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">OutputStreamWriter</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">out</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"UTF-8"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">bytes</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"ISO-8859-1"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="n">log</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">charset</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">name</span><span class="o">());</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h3 id="prefer-this">Prefer this…</h3>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">OutputStreamWriter</span> <span class="n">writer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">OutputStreamWriter</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">out</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">UTF_8</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">bytes</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">ISO_8859_1</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="n">log</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">charset</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("PreferCharsetOverload")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>If you call duration.getNanos(), you must also call duration.getSeconds() in ‘nearby’ code. If you are trying to convert this duration to nanoseconds, you probably meant to use Durations.toNanos(duration) instead.</p>

      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            QualifierOrScopeOnInjectMethod<br>
            <small>Qualifiers/Scope annotations on @Inject methods don't have any effect. Move the qualifier annotation to the binding location.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>LikelyError</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Inject</code> annotation is applied to <strong>injection points</strong> - methods,
constructors, or fields that a dependency injection tool like Guice or Dagger
will invoke or populate to construct an object.</p>

<p>Scope annotations (annotations that are themselves annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@ScopeAnnotation</code>) are used to denote the ‘effective scope’ of an object.
Examples of scope annotations include <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Singleton</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@RequestScope</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SessionScope</code>. These annotations can be used either on the declaration of a
type (so that every instantiation of that object will be handled with the
appropriate scope), or on a <strong>provider method</strong> (to declare that the particular
binding declared by that provider method is subject to that annotation’s scoping
rules):</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Singleton</span>
<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">ExpensiveGlobalObject</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">ExpensiveGlobalObject</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">SomeDependencies</span> <span class="n">stuff</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{...}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">SomeModule</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">AbstractModule</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
    <span class="nd">@Provides</span>
    <span class="nd">@Singleton</span>
    <span class="nc">OtherExpensiveObject</span> <span class="nf">provideOtherExpensiveObject</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Gold</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Qualifier annotations (annotations that are themselves annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Qualifier</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@BindingAnnotation</code>) are used to distinguish different
instances of the same type of object (the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Red Robot</code> instead of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Blue
Robot</code>). These annotations can be used <em>inside</em> injection points, or on those
provider methods:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">RobotArena</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">RobotArena</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nd">@Red</span> <span class="nc">Robot</span> <span class="n">redBot</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nd">@Blue</span> <span class="nc">Robot</span> <span class="n">blueBot</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{...}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">SomeModule</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">AbstractModule</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
    <span class="nd">@Provides</span>
    <span class="nd">@Red</span>
    <span class="nc">Robot</span> <span class="nf">provideRedRobot</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Robot</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"red"</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Notably: there is no method declaration where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Inject</code> and either a scope or a
qualifier annotation can reasonably coexist. Either the method is an <strong>injection
point</strong>, and the dependency injection system will ignore the scope or qualifier
annotation, or the method is a <strong>provider</strong> method, and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Inject</code> method
won’t have any effect, as modules are constructed without a dependency injection
container.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Example</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Here, @Singleton is ignored. Perhaps the scope should go onto Example, to make dependency</span>
  <span class="c1">// injection systems treat the Example type as a singleton.</span>
  <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nd">@Singleton</span>
  <span class="nc">Example</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Robot</span> <span class="n">something</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">MyModule</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">AbstractModule</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="c1">// The `@Inject` doesn't do anything: Guice will use this method to define a Singleton binding</span>
  <span class="c1">// for Database. When a Database is constructed by Guice, a DatabaseCredentials will be</span>
  <span class="c1">// constructed and this method will be invoked, but it isn't invoked until then.</span>
  <span class="nd">@Provides</span> <span class="nd">@Singleton</span> <span class="nd">@Inject</span>
  <span class="nc">Database</span> <span class="nf">providesSingletonDatabase</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">DatabaseCredentials</span> <span class="n">db</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("QualifierOrScopeOnInjectMethod")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            RecordComponentOverride<br>
            <small>@Override annotations on record components don't do anything.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Because <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Override</code> is a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Target(METHOD)</code> annotation, it’s automatically
permitted on record component declarations. It would normally cause the
annotation to be copied to the generated accessor method, but in this case it’s
a SOURCE-retention annotation so there’s nothing to do, and the annotation is
ignored.</p>

<p>Note that the annotation <em>does not</em> mean that the generated accessor method for
the record is overriding something.</p>

<p>Also note that a hand-written accessor method in a record class can also always
use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Override</code> regardless of supertype methods (see <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-9.html#jls-9.6.4.4">JLS §9.6.4.4</a>):</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>If a method declaration in class or interface Q is annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Override</code>,
then one of the following three conditions must be true, or a compile-time
error occurs:</p>

  <p>…</p>

  <p>Q is a record class (§8.10), and the method is an accessor method for a record
component of Q (§8.10.3)</p>
</blockquote>

<p>For additional discussion, see
<a href="https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/compiler-dev/2021-July/017602.html">this compile-dev@ thread</a>
and
<a href="https://github.com/google/error-prone/issues/5174">Error Prone issue #5174</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("RecordComponentOverride")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            RedundantControlFlow<br>
            <small>This continue statement is redundant and can be removed. It may be misleading.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Unnecessary control flow statements may be misleading in some contexts.</p>

<p>For instance, this method to find groups of prime order has a bug:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">filterGroupsOfPrimeOrder</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Iterable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">filtered</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Group</span> <span class="n">group</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="n">group</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">order</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="n">i</span><span class="o">++)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">order</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">%</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
        <span class="k">continue</span><span class="o">;</span>
      <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">continue</code> statement only breaks out of the innermost loop, so the input is
returned unchanged.</p>

<p>The most readable alternative is probably to avoid a nested loop entirely:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">filterGroupsOfPrimeOrder</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Iterable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">filtered</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Group</span> <span class="n">group</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">isPrime</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">order</span><span class="o">()))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">continue</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>A labelled break statement would also be correct, but is quite uncommon:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">filterGroupsOfPrimeOrder</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Iterable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Group</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">filtered</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="nl">outer:</span>
  <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Group</span> <span class="n">group</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">groups</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="n">group</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">order</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="n">i</span><span class="o">++)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">order</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">%</span> <span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
        <span class="k">continue</span> <span class="n">outer</span><span class="o">;</span>
      <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">group</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">filtered</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("RedundantControlFlow")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            RefactorSwitch<br>
            <small>This switch can be refactored to be more readable</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This checker aims to improve the readability of new-style arrow <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es by
simplifying and refactoring them.</p>

<h3 id="simplifications">Simplifications:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>When a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> consists only of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">yield</code>ing some value, it can be re-written
with just the value. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case FOO -&gt; { yield "bar"; }</code> can be
shortened to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case FOO -&gt; "bar";</code></li>
  <li>When a case has redundant braces around the right-hand side of the arrow,
they can be removed. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case FOO -&gt; { System.out.println("bar");
}</code> can shortened to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case FOO -&gt; System.out.println("bar");</code></li>
</ul>

<h3 id="factoring-out-return-switch">Factoring out <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return switch</code>:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>When every value of an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">enum</code> is covered by a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> which <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return</code>s, the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return</code> can be factored out</li>
</ul>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum SideOfCoin {OBVERSE, REVERSE};

private String renderName(SideOfCoin sideOfCoin) {
  switch(sideOfCoin) {
    case OBVERSE -&gt; {
      return "Heads";
    }
    case REVERSE -&gt; {
      return "Tails";
    }
  }
  // This should never happen, but removing this will cause a compile-time error
  throw new RuntimeException("Unknown side of coin");
}
</code></pre>

<p>The transformed code is simpler and elides the “should never happen” handler.</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum SideOfCoin {OBVERSE, REVERSE};

private String renderName(SideOfCoin sideOfCoin) {
  return switch(sideOfCoin) {
    case OBVERSE -&gt; "Heads";
    case REVERSE -&gt; "Tails";
  };
}
</code></pre>

<ul>
  <li>When switching on something other than an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">enum</code>, if the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s are
exhaustive, then a similar refactoring can be performed.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="factoring-out-assignment-switch">Factoring out assignment <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>When every <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> just assigns a value to the same variable, the assignment
can potentially be factored out</li>
  <li>If a local variable is defined and then immediately overwritten by a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>, the definition and assignment can potentially be combined</li>
</ul>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void updateScore(Suit suit) {
  int score = 0;
  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS, DIAMONDS -&gt; {
      score = -1;
    }
    case SPADES -&gt; {
      score = 2;
    }
    case CLUBS -&gt; {
      score = 3;
    }
  }
}
</code></pre>

<p>Which can be consolidated:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void updateScore(Suit suit) {
   int score = switch(suit) {
       case HEARTS, DIAMONDS -&gt; -1;
       case SPADES -&gt; 2;
       case CLUBS -&gt; 3;
    };
}
</code></pre>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("RefactorSwitch")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ReferenceEquality<br>
            <small>Comparison using reference equality instead of value equality</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Reference types should normally be compared for value equality with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code>,
not for object identity with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">==</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">!=</code>.</p>

<h2 id="faqs">FAQs</h2>

<h3 id="what-if-i-know-that-this-classs-equals-method-uses-object-identity-anyway">What if I know that this class’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code> method uses object identity anyway?</h3>

<p>This check allows you to use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">==</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">!=</code> in cases in which it can reliably
determine that they would behave identically to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code>, such as for enums or
for final classes that inherit the default <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code> implementation from
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>. You might prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">==</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">!=</code> in such cases, since it is less
verbose, especially compared to using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Objects.equals(a, b)</code> in cases in which
you need to tolerate null values.</p>

<h3 id="how-about-comparing-interned-objects">How about comparing interned objects?</h3>

<p>It’s dangerous to rely on your instances being interned. We have no tooling to
check or enforce that, and it’s easy to get wrong.</p>

<h3 id="but-what-about-boolean-values-we-know-theres-just-true-and-false-and-null-surely-theyre-okay">But what about <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Boolean</code> values? We <em>know</em> there’s just <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TRUE</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">FALSE</code> (and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>). Surely <em>they’re</em> okay!</h3>

<p>Well, no, because some tricky client can always generate a new instance with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">new Boolean(true)</code>. Comparing with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> always works; comparing with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">==</code>
doesn’t.</p>

<h3 id="how-about-a-reference-equality-comparison-before-a-more-expensive-content-equality-comparison">How about a reference equality comparison before a more expensive content equality comparison?</h3>

<p>The check allows implementations of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object#equals()</code> to perform reference
equality tests on the type equality is being implemented for. For example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>abstract class Foo {

  abstract String bar();

  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if (this == other) {
      return true; // fast path, reference equality is allowed here
    }
    if (!(other instanceof Foo)) {
      return false;
    }
    Foo that = (Foo) other;
    // value equality should still be used for types other than `Foo`
    return bar().equals(that.bar());
  }
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>In other cases, calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Type#equals()</code> should be just as fast, because that
method will likely be inlined, and the first thing it will likely do is that
same instance comparison.</p>

<p>Alternatively, if you’re okay with accepting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code>, you could call
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.Objects.equals()</code>, which first does a reference equality comparison
and then falls back to content equality for non-null arguments.</p>

<h3 id="how-about-asserting-in-a-test-that-two-different-references-point-to-the-same-object-or-not">How about asserting in a test that two different references point to the same object (or not)?</h3>

<p>Assertion libraries provide clearer ways to assert this, with the bonus of
providing better failure messages:</p>

<p>Truth:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>assertThat(a).isSameInstanceAs(b);
assertThat(a).isNotSameInstanceAs(b);
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>AssertJ:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>assertThat(a).isSameAs(b);
assertThat(a).isNotSameAs(b);
</code></pre></div></div>

<h3 id="how-about-comparing-against-a-special-marker-instance">How about comparing against a special marker instance?</h3>

<p>Classes override <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> to express when two instances should be treated as
interchangeable with each other. Predominant Java libraries and practices are
built on that assumption. Defining a “magic instance” for such a type goes
against this whole practice, leaving you vulnerable to unexpected bugs.</p>

<p>Consider choosing a sentinel value within the domain of the type (the moral
equivalent of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-1</code> for indexOf function calls) that you could compare against
using the normal <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> method.</p>

<h3 id="so-how-can-i-put-a-special-nothing-value-in-my-map">So how can I put a special “nothing” value in my map?</h3>

<p>Use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Optional&lt;V&gt;</code> as the value type of your map instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ReferenceEquality")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

            RethrowReflectiveOperationExceptionAsLinkageError<br>
            <small>Prefer LinkageError for rethrowing ReflectiveOperationException as unchecked</small>
          </h1>
        </div>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Consider using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">LinkageError</code> instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AssertionError</code> when rethrowing
reflective exceptions as unchecked exceptions, since it conveys more information
when reflection fails due to an incompatible change in the classpath.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("RethrowReflectiveOperationExceptionAsLinkageError")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ReturnAtTheEndOfVoidFunction<br>
            <small>`return;` is unnecessary at the end of void methods and constructors.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Detects no-op <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return</code> statements in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">void</code> functions when they occur at the end
of the method.</p>

<p>Instead of:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">stuff</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">5</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="k">return</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>do:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">stuff</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">x</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">5</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ReturnAtTheEndOfVoidFunction")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            RxReturnValueIgnored<br>
            <small>Returned Rx objects must be checked. Ignoring a returned Rx value means it is never scheduled for execution</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Methods that return an ignored [Observable | Single | Flowable | Maybe ] generally indicate errors.</p>

<p>If you don’t check the return value of these methods, the observables may never execute. It also means the error case is not being handled</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("RxReturnValueIgnored")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ScannerUseDelimiter<br>
            <small>Scanner.useDelimiter is not an efficient way to read an entire InputStream</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Scanner.useDelimiter("\\A")</code> is not an efficient way to read an entire
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">InputStream</code>.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Scanner</span> <span class="n">scanner</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Scanner</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">inputStream</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">UTF_8</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">useDelimiter</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"\\A"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">scanner</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasNext</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">scanner</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">next</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="s">""</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Scanner</code> separates its input into “tokens” based on a delimiter that is a
regular expression. The regular expression <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\A</code> matches the beginning of the
input, only, so there is no later delimiter and the single token consists of
every character read from the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">InputStream</code>.</p>

<p>This works, but has multiple drawbacks:</p>

<ul>
  <li>You need a special case for an empty <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">InputStream</code>. In that case there is no
token after <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\A</code>. That’s why the extract above checks <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hasNext()</code>. If you
forget to do that, you get <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NoSuchElementException</code> in the empty case.</li>
  <li>
    <p>It swallows <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IOException</code>. Quoting the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Scanner</code> specification:</p>

    <blockquote>
      <p>A scanner can read text from any object which implements the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Readable</code>
interface. If an invocation of the underlying readable’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">read()</code> method
throws an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IOException</code> then the scanner assumes that the end of the input
has been reached. The most recent <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IOException</code> thrown by the underlying
readable can be retrieved via the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ioException()</code> method.</p>
    </blockquote>
  </li>
  <li>It is much slower than calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">inputStream.readAllBytes()</code>.</li>
</ul>

<p>Instead, prefer one of the following alternatives:</p>

<p>Since Java 9, it has been possible to write this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">inputStream</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">readAllBytes</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="no">UTF_8</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>On Android, that does require API level 33, though. Guava’s
<a href="https://guava.dev/releases/snapshot-jre/api/docs/com/google/common/io/ByteStreams.html#toByteArray\(java.io.InputStream\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ByteStreams.toByteArray(inputStream)</code></a>
is equivalent to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">inputStream.readAllBytes()</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ScannerUseDelimiter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SelfAlwaysReturnsThis<br>
            <small>Non-abstract instance methods named 'self()' or 'getThis()' that return the enclosing class must always 'return this'</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A common pattern for abstract <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Builders</code> is to declare an instance method named
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">self()</code>, which subtypes override and implement as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return this</code> (see Effective
Java 3rd Edition, Item 2).</p>

<p>Returning anything other than <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">this</code> from an instance method named <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">self()</code> with
a return type that matches the enclosing class will be confusing for readers and
callers.</p>

<h2 id="casting">Casting</h2>

<p>If an unchecked cast is required, prefer a single-statement cast, with the
suppression on the method (rather than the statement). For example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="nd">@SuppressWarnings</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"unchecked"</span><span class="o">)</span>
  <span class="k">default</span> <span class="no">U</span> <span class="nf">self</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="no">U</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Instead of:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="k">default</span> <span class="no">U</span> <span class="nf">self</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nd">@SuppressWarnings</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"unchecked"</span><span class="o">)</span>
    <span class="no">U</span> <span class="n">self</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="no">U</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">self</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SelfAlwaysReturnsThis")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SelfSet<br>
            <small>This setter seems to be invoked with a value from its own getter. Is it redundant?</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>A setter invoked with a value from the corresponding getter is often a mistake,
for example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">from</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasFrobnicator</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">to</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">setFrobnicator</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">to</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getFrobnicator</span><span class="o">());</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This is easy to accidentally write, but is clearly meant to be,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">from</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasFrobnicator</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">to</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">setFrobnicator</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">from</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getFrobnicator</span><span class="o">());</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The Java proto API is tolerant enough that the former code will compile and
execute fine, but it will set <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">frobnicator</code> to the default value for that field.</p>

<p>This pattern is occasionally used to ensure that a field is always present, even
if it takes the default value, for example,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// ensure "always_present" is present</span>
<span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">setAlwaysPresent</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getAlwaysPresent</span><span class="o">());</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This is not a no-op, but we’d encourage being more explicit about the condition,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasAlwaysPresent</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">setAlwaysPresent</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Or if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">builder</code> is otherwise untouched, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">builder.setAlwaysPresent(false)</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SelfSet")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ShortCircuitBoolean<br>
            <small>Prefer the short-circuiting boolean operators && and || to & and |.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The boolean operators <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&amp;&amp;</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">||</code> should almost always be used instead of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&amp;</code>
and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">|</code>.</p>

<p>If the right hand side is an expression that has side effects or is expensive to
compute, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&amp;&amp;</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">||</code> will short-circuit but <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">&amp;</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">|</code> will not, which may be
surprising or cause slowness.</p>

<p>If evaluating both operands is necessary for side effects, consider refactoring
to make that explicit. For example, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="n">rhs</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">hasSideEffects</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">lhs</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="n">rhs</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">lhs</span> <span class="o">&amp;</span> <span class="n">hasSideEffects</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ShortCircuitBoolean")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            StatementSwitchToExpressionSwitch<br>
            <small>This statement switch can be converted to a new-style arrow switch</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>We’re trying to make <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es simpler to understand at a glance.
Misunderstanding the control flow of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> is a common source of bugs.</p>

<p>As part of this simplification, new-style arrow (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-&gt;</code>) switches are encouraged
instead of old-style colon (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">:</code>) switches. And where possible, neighboring cases
are grouped together (e.g. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case A, B, C</code>).</p>

<h3 id="old-style-colon--switches">Old-style colon (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">:</code>) <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>Have a colon between the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>’s code. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case
HEARTS:</code></li>
  <li>Because of the potential for fall-through, it takes time and cognitive load
to understand the control flow. When a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> block is large, just
skimming each <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> can be toilsome. Fall-through can also be conditional
(see example 5. below). In this scenario, one would potentially need to
reason about all possible flows for each <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>. When conditionally
falling-through multiple <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s, the number of potential control flows can
grow rapidly</li>
  <li>Lexical scopes overlap, which can lead to surprising behaviors: definitions
of local variables from earlier <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s are propagated down to later
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s, however the <em>values</em> that initialize those local variables do not
propagate in the same way</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="new-style-arrow---switches">New-style arrow (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-&gt;</code>) <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es:</h3>

<ul>
  <li>Have an arrow between the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>’s code. For example, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case
HEARTS -&gt;</code></li>
  <li>No <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s fall through; no control flow analysis needed</li>
  <li>Safely and easily reorder <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s (within a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>)</li>
  <li>Lexical scopes are isolated between different <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>s; if you define a local
variable within a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>, it can only be used within that specific <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="examples">Examples</h3>

<h4 id="1-eliminate-fall-through">1. Eliminate fall through</h4>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void foo(Suit suit) {
  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS:
      System.out.println("Red hearts");
      break;
    case DIAMONDS:
      System.out.println("Red diamonds");
      break;
    case SPADES:
    // Fall through
    case CLUBS:
      bar();
      System.out.println("Black suit");
    }
}
</code></pre>

<p>Which can be simplified by grouping and using a new-style switch:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void foo(Suit suit) {
  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS -&gt; System.out.println("Red hearts");
    case DIAMONDS -&gt; System.out.println("Red diamonds");
    case SPADES, CLUBS -&gt; {
      bar();
      System.out.println("Black suit");
    }
  }
}
</code></pre>

<h4 id="2-return-switch-">2. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return switch ...</code></h4>

<p>Sometimes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> is used with a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return</code> for each <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code>, like this:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum SideOfCoin {OBVERSE, REVERSE};

private String renderName(SideOfCoin sideOfCoin) {
  switch(sideOfCoin) {
    case OBVERSE:
      return "Heads";
    case REVERSE:
      return "Tails";
    }
    // This should never happen, but removing this will cause a compile-time error
    throw new RuntimeException("Unknown side of coin");
}
</code></pre>

<p>Note that even though a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> is present for each possible value of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">enum</code>,
a boilerplate “should never happen” clause is still needed. The transformed code
is simpler and doesn’t need a “should never happen” clause.</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>enum SideOfCoin {OBVERSE, REVERSE};

private String renderName(SideOfCoin sideOfCoin) {
  return switch(sideOfCoin) {
    case OBVERSE -&gt; "Heads";
    case REVERSE -&gt; "Tails";
  };
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If you nevertheless wish to define an explicit “should never happen” clause,
this can be accomplished by placing the logic inside a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">default</code> case. For
example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>enum SideOfCoin {OBVERSE, REVERSE};

private String foo(SideOfCoin sideOfCoin) {
  return switch(sideOfCoin) {
    case OBVERSE -&gt; "Heads";
    case REVERSE -&gt; "Tails";
    default -&gt; throw new RuntimeException("Unknown side of coin"); // should never happen
  };
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>When the checker detects an existing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">default</code> that appears to be redundant, it
may suggest a secondary auto-fix which removes the redundant <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">default</code> and its
code (if any).</p>

<h4 id="3-assignment-switch">3. Assignment <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code></h4>

<p>If every branch of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> is making an assignment to the same variable, the
code can be simplified into a combined assignment and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

int score = 0;

private void updateScore(Suit suit) {
  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS:
    // Fall thru
    case DIAMONDS:
      score += -1;
      break;
    case SPADES:
      score += 2;
      break;
    case CLUBS:
      score += 3;
    }
}
</code></pre>

<p>This can be simplified as follows:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

int score = 0;

private void updateScore(Suit suit) {
  score += switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS, DIAMONDS -&gt; -1;
    case SPADES -&gt; 2;
    case CLUBS -&gt; 3;
  };
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Taking this one step further: if a local variable is defined, and then
immediately followed by a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> in which every <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">case</code> assigns to that same
variable, then all three (the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>, the variable declaration, and the
assignment) can be merged:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void updateStatus(Suit suit) {
  int score;

  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS:
    // Fall thru
    case DIAMONDS:
      score = 1;
      break;
    case SPADES:
      score = 2;
      break;
    case CLUBS:
      score = 3;
    }
  ...

}
</code></pre>

<p>Becomes:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void updateStatus(Suit suit) {
  int score = switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS, DIAMONDS -&gt; 1;
    case SPADES -&gt; 2;
    case CLUBS -&gt; 3;
  };
  ...
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<h4 id="4-just-converting-to-new-arrow-switch">4. Just converting to new arrow <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code></h4>

<p>Even when the simplifications discussed above are not applicable, conversion to
new arrow <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es can be automated by this checker:</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void processEvent(Suit suit) {
    switch (suit) {
      case CLUBS:
        String message = "hello";
        var anotherMessage = "salut";
        processMessages(message, anotherMessage);
        break;
      case DIAMONDS:
        anotherMessage = "bonjour";
        processMessage(anotherMessage);
    }
}
</code></pre>

<p>Note that the local variables referenced in multiple cases are hoisted up out of
the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> statement, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">var</code> declarations are converted to explicit types,
resulting in:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private void processEvent(Suit suit) {
    String anotherMessage;
    switch (suit) {
      case CLUBS -&gt; {
        String message = "hello";
        anotherMessage = "salut";
        processMessages(message, anotherMessage);
      }
      case DIAMONDS -&gt; {
        anotherMessage = "bonjour";
        processMessage(anotherMessage);
      }
    }
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<h4 id="5-complex-control-flows">5. Complex control flows</h4>

<p>Here’s an example of a complex statement <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code> with conditional fall-through
and various control flows. Unfortunately, the checker does not currently have
the ability to automatically convert such code to new-style arrow <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">switch</code>es.
Manually converting the code could be a good opportunity to improve its
readability.</p>

<p>How many potential execution paths can you spot?</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">enum Suit {HEARTS, CLUBS, SPADES, DIAMONDS};

private int foo(Suit suit){
  switch(suit) {
    case HEARTS:
      if (bar()) {
        break;
      }
    // Fall through
    case CLUBS:
      if (baz()) {
        return 1;
      } else if (baz2()) {
        throw new AssertionError(...);
      }
    // Fall through
    case SPADES:
    // Fall through
    case DIAMONDS:
      return 0;
  }
  return -1;
}
</code></pre>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StatementSwitchToExpressionSwitch")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    <div class="container">
