        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            StaticAssignmentInConstructor<br>
            <small>This assignment is to a static field. Mutating static state from a constructor is highly error-prone.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Assigning to a static variable from a constructor is highly indicative of a bug,
or error-prone design.</p>

<p>Common reasons are:</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p>The field simply should be an instance field, and there’s a bug.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>An attempt is being made to lazily initialize a static field. In this case,
first consider whether lazy initialization is necessary: it often isn’t. If
it is, doing it from a constructor is very hairy: the static field could be
accessed from a static method before the class is even initialized. Consider
using a memoized <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Supplier</code>.</p>
  </li>
</ol>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticAssignmentInConstructor")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            StaticAssignmentOfThrowable<br>
            <small>Saving instances of Throwable in static fields is discouraged, prefer to create them on-demand when an exception is thrown</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The problem we’re trying to prevent is unhelpful stack traces that don’t contain
information about where the Exception was thrown from. This problem can
sometimes arise when an attempt is being made to cache or reuse a Throwable
(often, a particular Exception). In this case, consider whether this is really
is necessary: it often isn’t. Could a Throwable simply be instantiated when
needed?</p>

<pre><code class="language-{.bad}">// this always has the same stack trace
static final MyException MY_EXCEPTION = new MyException("something terrible has happened!");
</code></pre>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">throw new MyException("something terrible has happened!");
</code></pre>

<pre><code class="language-{.good}">static MyException myException() {
 return new MyException("something terrible has happened!");
}
</code></pre>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticAssignmentOfThrowable")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            StaticGuardedByInstance<br>
            <small>Writes to static fields should not be guarded by instance locks</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Protecting writes to a static field by synchronizing on an instance lock is not
thread-safe.</p>

<p>In the following example, two difference instances of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Test</code> can each acquire
their own instance lock and call <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">initialize()</code> at the same time.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Test</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">lock</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Object</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="n">initialized</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">initialize</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="cm">/* ... */</span> <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="nc">Test</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">lock</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">initialized</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
        <span class="n">initialize</span><span class="o">();</span>
        <span class="c1">// error: modification of static variable guarded by instance variable 'lock'</span>
        <span class="n">initialized</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">;</span>
      <span class="o">}</span>
      <span class="c1">// ...</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Static fields should generally be guarded by static locks, and instance fields
guarded by instance locks.</p>

<p>The example above could be made thread-safe by locking on the enclosing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Class</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Test</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">initialized</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">initialize</span><span class="o">();</span>
    <span class="n">initialized</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To update a static counter from an instance method, consider using
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/atomic/AtomicInteger.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AtomicInteger</code></a>
instead of incrementing a static <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">int</code> field.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticGuardedByInstance")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            StaticMockMember<br>
            <small>@Mock members of test classes shouldn't share state between tests and preferably be non-static</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Making a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Mock</code> instance <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code> will share the state across tests and can
make them order dependent and/or unclear to reader/maintainer. Removing
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code>, will ensure fresh mock instances are used for each tests.</p>

<p>Additionally, if the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Mock</code> instance is marked as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code> to make it
serializable, there is a cleaner way to do it :
https://javadoc.io/doc/org.mockito/mockito-core/latest/org/mockito/Mockito.html#serilization_across_classloader
and
https://javadoc.io/static/org.mockito/mockito-core/3.3.3/org/mockito/Mock.html#serializable–</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticMockMember")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            StreamResourceLeak<br>
            <small>Streams that encapsulate a closeable resource should be closed using try-with-resources</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: FilesLinesLeak</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The problem is described in the <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/nio/file/Files.html">javadoc</a> for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files</code>.</p>

<h2 id="filesnewdirectorystream"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.newDirectoryStream</code></h2>

<blockquote>
  <p>When not using the try-with-resources construct, then directory stream’s close
method should be invoked after iteration is completed so as to free any
resources held for the open directory.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="fileslist"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.list</code></h2>

<blockquote>
  <p>The returned stream encapsulates a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DirectoryStream</code>. If timely disposal of
file system resources is required, the try-with-resources construct should be
used to ensure that the stream’s close method is invoked after the stream
operations are completed.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="fileswalk"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.walk</code></h2>

<blockquote>
  <p>The returned stream encapsulates one or more <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DirectoryStreams</code>. If timely
disposal of file system resources is required, the try-with-resources
construct should be used to ensure that the stream’s close method is invoked
after the stream operations are completed. Operating on a closed stream will
result in an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IllegalStateException</code>.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="filesfind"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.find</code></h2>

<blockquote>
  <p>The returned stream encapsulates one or more <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DirectoryStreams</code>. If timely
disposal of file system resources is required, the try-with-resources
construct should be used to ensure that the stream’s close method is invoked
after the stream operations are completed. Operating on a closed stream will
result in an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IllegalStateException</code>.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="fileslines"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.lines</code></h2>

<blockquote>
  <p>The returned stream encapsulates a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Reader</code>. If timely disposal of file system
resources is required, the try-with-resources construct should be used to
ensure that the stream’s close method is invoked after the stream operations
are completed.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="the-solution">The solution</h2>

<p>To ensure the stream is closed, always use try-with-resources. For example, when
using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Files.lines</code>, do this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">input</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Stream</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">stream</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Files</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">lines</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="o">))</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">input</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">stream</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">collect</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Collectors</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">joining</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">", "</span><span class="o">));</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Not this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// the Reader is never closed!</span>
<span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">input</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Files</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">lines</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">collect</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Collectors</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">joining</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">", "</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="must-be-closed">What about methods that return closeable streams?</h2>

<p>Methods that return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code>s that encapsulate a closeable resource can be
annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations.MustBeClosed</code> to ensure their
callers remember to close the stream.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StreamResourceLeak")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            StreamToIterable<br>
            <small>Using stream::iterator creates a one-shot Iterable, which may cause surprising failures.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">stream::iterator</code> to create an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> results in an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> which
can only be iterated once, and will throw an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IllegalArgumentException</code> on
subsequent attempts.</p>

<p>The contract of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> is poorly defined, but many APIs will assume that
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code>s allow multiple iteration.</p>

<p>To give a concrete example using protocol buffers,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">MyProto</span> <span class="nf">construct</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Stream</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">()</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">addAllSubMessage</span><span class="o">(</span>
          <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">SubMessage</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setVal</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">())::</span><span class="n">iterator</span><span class="o">)</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>With the current implementation of the protocol buffer generated code, this will
work, but the following minor change will lead to re-iteration and failure,</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">MyProto</span> <span class="nf">construct</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Stream</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span> <span class="n">builder</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">addSubMessageBuilder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setVal</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">builder</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">addAllSubMessage</span><span class="o">(</span>
          <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">SubMessage</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setVal</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">())::</span><span class="n">iterator</span><span class="o">)</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span> <span class="c1">// build iterates twice, and throws.</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To avoid such pitfalls, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code> can either be terminated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">forEachOrdered</code></p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">MyProto</span> <span class="nf">construct</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Stream</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span> <span class="n">builder</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">SubMessage</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setVal</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">())</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">forEachOrdered</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nl">builder:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">addSubMessage</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>or collected (with the caveat that the contents of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code> will now be
materialized into memory at once),</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">MyProto</span> <span class="nf">construct</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Stream</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nc">MyProto</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">()</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">addAllSubMessage</span><span class="o">(</span>
          <span class="n">ints</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">map</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">SubMessage</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">newBuilder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setVal</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">i</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">())</span>
              <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">collect</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">toImmutableList</span><span class="o">()))</span>
      <span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>or suppressed using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StreamToIterable")</code>. Only suppress if
you’re sure the API you’re using will only iterate the resulting one-shot
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> once, and can’t accept a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream</code> or an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterator</code>.</p>


    </div>

          <h1>
            StringCaseLocaleUsage<br>
            <small>Specify a `Locale` when calling `String#to{Lower,Upper}Case`. (Note: there are multiple suggested fixes; the third may be most appropriate if you're dealing with ASCII Strings.)</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String.toLowerCase()</code> (and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">toUpperCase</code>) without specifying a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Locale</code> can
have surprising results.</p>

<p>For example, if this is used on a device and the user’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Locale</code> is Türkiye,
then <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"I".toLowerCase()</code> will yield a lowercase dotless I (“ı”). This could be
extremely dangerous if you were expecting to operate on ASCII text to generate
machine-readable identifiers.</p>

<p>If this kind of regionalisation is desired, use
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.toLowerCase(Locale.getDefault())</code> to make that explicit. If not,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">.toLowerCase(Locale.ENGLISH)</code> will give you
casing independent of the user’s current <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Locale</code>. If you know that you’re
operating on ASCII, prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Ascii.toLower/UpperCase</code> to make that explicit.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StringCaseLocaleUsage")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            StringConcatToTextBlock<br>
            <small>This string literal can be written more clearly as a text block</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Using <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/text-blocks/index.html">text blocks</a> for strings that span multiple lines can make code easier to
read.</p>

<p>For example, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">message</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="s">"""
    'The time has come,' the Walrus said,
    'To talk of many things:
    Of shoes -- and ships -- and sealing-wax --
    Of cabbages -- and kings --
    And why the sea is boiling hot --
    And whether pigs have wings.'
    """</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>instead of this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">message</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="s">"'The time has come,' the Walrus said,\n"</span>
        <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"'To talk of many things:\n"</span>
        <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"Of shoes -- and ships -- and sealing-wax --\n"</span>
        <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"Of cabbages -- and kings --\n"</span>
        <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"And why the sea is boiling hot --\n"</span>
        <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"And whether pigs have wings.'\n"</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="trailing-newlines">Trailing newlines</h2>

<p>If the string should not contain a trailing newline, use a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\ </code> to escape the
final newline in the text block. That is, these two strings are equivalent:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"hello\n"</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="s">"world"</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="s">"""
    hello
    world\
    """</span><span class="o">;</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The suggested fixes for this check preserve the exact contents of the original
string, so if the original string doesn’t include a trailing newline the fix
will use a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\ </code> to escape the last newline.</p>

<p>If the whitespace in the string isn’t significant, for example because the
string value will be parsed by a parser that doesn’t care about the trailing
newlines, consider removing the final <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\ </code> to improve the readability of the
string.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StringConcatToTextBlock")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            StringSplitter<br>
            <small>String.split(String) has surprising behavior</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String.split(String)</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pattern.split(CharSequence)</code> have surprising
behaviour. For example, consider the following puzzler from
https://konigsberg.blogspot.com/2009/11/final-thoughts-java-puzzler-splitting.html:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">nothing</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">""</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">split</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">":"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">bunchOfNothing</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">":"</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">split</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">":"</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The result is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[""]</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[]</code>!</p>

<p>More examples:</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>input</th>
      <th><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">input.split(":")</code></th>
      <th><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pattern.compile(":").split(input)</code></th>
      <th><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Splitter.on(':').split(input)</code></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">""</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[""]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[""]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[""]</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">":"</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["", ""]</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">":::"</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">[]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["", "", "", ""]</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"a:::"</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["a"]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["a"]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["a", "", "", ""]</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">":::b"</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["", "", "", "b"]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["", "", "", "b"]</code></td>
      <td><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">["", "", "", "b"]</code></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>Prefer either:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>Guava’s
<a href="https://guava.dev/releases/23.0/api/docs/com/google/common/base/Splitter.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Splitter</code></a>,
which has less surprising behaviour and provides explicit control over the
handling of empty strings and the trimming of whitespace with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">trimResults</code>
and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">omitEmptyStrings</code>.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/String.html#split\(java.lang.String,int\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String.split(String, int)</code></a>
or
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/String.html#split\(java.lang.String,int\)"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pattern.split(CharSequence, int)</code></a>
and setting an explicit ‘limit’ to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-1</code> to match the behaviour of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Splitter</code>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>TIP: if you use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Splitter</code>, consider extracting the instance to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code>
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> field.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StringSplitter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SuperCallToObjectMethod<br>
            <small>`super.equals(obj)` and `super.hashCode()` are often bugs when they call the methods defined in `java.lang.Object`</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>LikelyError</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: SuperEqualsIsObjectEquals</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Implementations of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> should usually not delegate to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.hashCode</code>.</p>

<p>Those two methods implement equality based on object identity. That
implementation <em>is</em> sometimes what the author intended. (This check attempts to
identify those cases and <em>not</em> report a warning for them. But in some cases, it
still produces a warning when it shouldn’t.)</p>

<p>But when <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">super.equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">super.hashCode</code> call the methods defined in
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>, the developer often did <em>not</em> intend to use object identity. Often,
developers write something like:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">obj</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="kd">super</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="o">((</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="kd">super</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">^</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This appears to be an attempt to define equality in terms of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">id</code> field in
this class and any fields in the superclass. However, when the superclass that
defines <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> is <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object</code>, the code instead defines equality in
terms of a mix of object identity and field values. The result is equivalent to
defining it in terms of identity alone—which is equivalent to not overriding
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode</code> at all!</p>

<p>Typically, the code should be rewritten to remove the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">super</code> calls entirely:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">obj</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="o">((</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Note that the suggested edits for this check instead preserve behavior, which
likely means preserving bugs! However, in cases in which object identity <em>is</em>
intended, we recommend applying the suggested edit to make that behavior
explicit in the code:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// This class's definition of equality is unusual and perhaps not ideal.</span>
<span class="c1">// But it is at least explicit.</span>

<span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Integer</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Object</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">obj</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">this</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(((</span><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="n">obj</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">id</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">;</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nd">@Override</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="kc">null</span> <span class="o">?</span> <span class="n">id</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">identityHashCode</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SuperCallToObjectMethod")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SwigMemoryLeak<br>
            <small>SWIG generated code that can't call a C++ destructor will leak memory</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>SWIG is a tool that will automatically generate Java bindings to C++ code. It is
possible to %ignore in SWIG a C++ object’s destructor, this is trivially
achieved when using %ignoreall and then selectively %unignore-ing an API. SWIG
cleans up C++ objects using a delete method, which is most commonly called by a
finalizer. When a SWIG generated delete method can’t call a destructor, as it is
hidden, the delete method throws an exception. However, in the case of a hidden
C++ destructor SWIG also doesn’t generate a finalizer, and so the most common
call to the delete method is removed. The consequence of this is that the SWIG
objects leak their C++ counterpart and no warnings or exceptions are thrown.</p>

<p>This check looks for the pattern of a memory leaking SWIG generated object and
warns about the potential memory leak. The most straightforward fix is to the
SWIG input code to tell it not to %ignore the C++ code’s destructor.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SwigMemoryLeak")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SynchronizeOnNonFinalField<br>
            <small>Synchronizing on non-final fields is not safe: if the field is ever updated, different threads may end up locking on different objects.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Possible fixes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>If the field is never reassigned, add the missing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> modifier.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>If the field needs to be mutable, create a separate lock by adding a private
final field and synchronizing on it to guard all accesses.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>If the field is lazily initialized, annotation it with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">com.google.errorprone.annotations.concurrent.LazyInit</code>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SynchronizeOnNonFinalField")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>
    <footer class="footer">

    <div class="col-lg-12">
      <p class="text-muted">&copy; 2026 Google</p>

      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            SystemConsoleNull<br>
            <small>System.console() no longer returns null in JDK 22 and newer versions</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Null-checking <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.console()</code> is not a reliable way to detect if the console
is connected to a terminal.</p>

<p>See JDK 22
<a href="https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8309155">Release Note: JLine As The Default Console Provider</a>:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.console()</code> now returns a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Console</code> object when the standard streams
are redirected or connected to a virtual terminal. In prior releases,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.console()</code> returned <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> for these cases. This change may impact
code that uses the return from <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.console()</code> to test if the VM is
connected to a terminal. If needed, running with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-Djdk.console=java.base</code>
will restore older behavior where the console is only returned when it is
connected to a terminal.</p>
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
  <p>A new method <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Console.isTerminal()</code> has been added to test if console is
connected to a terminal.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>and JDK 25 release note
<a href="https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8351576">Release Note: Default Console Implementation No Longer Based On JLine</a>:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>The default Console obtained via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.console()</code> is no longer based on
JLine. Since JDK 20, the JDK has included a JLine-based Console
implementation, offering a richer user experience and better support for
virtual terminal environments, such as IDEs. This implementation was initially
opt-in via a system property in JDK 20 and JDK 21 and became the default in
JDK 22. However, maintaining the JLine-based Console proved challenging. As a
result, in JDK 25, it has reverted to being opt-in, as it was in JDK 20 and
JDK 21.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>To prepare for this change while remaining compatible with JDK versions prior to
JDK 22, consider using reflection to call <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Console#isTerminal</code> on JDK versions
that support it:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="nd">@SuppressWarnings</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"SystemConsoleNull"</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="c1">// https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/SystemConsoleNull</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">systemConsoleIsTerminal</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">Console</span> <span class="n">systemConsole</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">console</span><span class="o">();</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Runtime</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">version</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">feature</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="mi">22</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="n">systemConsole</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">systemConsole</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">;</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
    <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">return</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="nc">Console</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMethod</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"isTerminal"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">invoke</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">systemConsole</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ReflectiveOperationException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
      <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">LinkageError</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMessage</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SystemConsoleNull")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ThreadJoinLoop<br>
            <small>Thread.join needs to be immediately surrounded by a loop until it succeeds. Consider using Uninterruptibles.joinUninterruptibly.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Thread.join() can be interrupted, and so requires users to catch
InterruptedException. Most users should be looping until the join() actually
succeeds.</p>

<p>Instead of writing your own try-catch and loop to handle it properly, you may
use <strong>Uninterruptibles.joinUninterruptibly</strong> which does the same for you.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>Thread thread = new Thread(new Runnable() {...});

Uninterruptibles.joinUninterruptibly(thread);
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ThreadJoinLoop")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ThreadLocalUsage<br>
            <small>ThreadLocals should be stored in static fields</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code>s should be stored in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code> variables to avoid memory leaks. If
a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code> is stored in an instance (non-static) variable, there will be
<code>M \* N</code> instances of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ThreadLocal</code> value where <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">M</code> is the number
of threads, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">N</code> is the number of instances of the containing class. Each
instance may remain live as long the thread that stored it stays live.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">C</span> <span class="o">{</span>
   <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">D</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">local</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">D</span><span class="o">&gt;();</span>

   <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nf">f</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
       <span class="no">D</span> <span class="n">d</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">local</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">();</span>
       <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">d</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
          <span class="n">d</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="no">D</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">);</span>
          <span class="n">local</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">set</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">d</span><span class="o">);</span>
       <span class="o">}</span>
       <span class="n">d</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">doSomething</span><span class="o">();</span>
   <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>The fix is often to make the field <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">D</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">local</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">ThreadLocal</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">D</span><span class="o">&gt;();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ThreadLocalUsage")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            ThreadPriorityCheck<br>
            <small>Relying on the thread scheduler is discouraged.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Don’t rely on the thread scheduler for correctness or performance. Instead,
ensure that the average number of runnable threads is not significantly greater
than the number of processors, i.e. by using the executor framework and an
appropriately sized thread pool.</p>

<p>For more information, see <a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=BIpDDwAAQBAJ">Effective Java 3rd Edition §84</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ThreadPriorityCheck")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ThreeLetterTimeZoneID<br>
            <small>Three-letter time zone identifiers are deprecated, may be ambiguous, and might not do what you intend; the full IANA time zone ID should be used instead.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>According to the Javadoc of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.TimeZone</code>:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>For compatibility with JDK 1.1.x, some other three-letter time zone IDs (such
as “PST”, “CTT”, “AST”) are also supported. However, their use is deprecated
because the same abbreviation is often used for multiple time zones (for
example, “CST” could be U.S. “Central Standard Time” and “China Standard
Time”), and the Java platform can then only recognize one of them.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Aside from the ambiguity between timezones, there is inconsistency in the
observance of Daylight Savings Time for the returned time zone, meaning the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TimeZone</code> obtained may not be what you expect. Examples include:</p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateTime.getTimeZone("PST")</code> does observe daylight savings time; however,
the identifier implies that it is Pacific <em>Standard</em> Time, i.e. daylight
savings time is not observed.</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">DateTime.getTimeZone("EST")</code> (and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"MST"</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"HST"</code>) do not observe
daylight savings time. However, this is inconsistent with PST (and others),
so you may believe that daylight savings time will be observed.</li>
</ul>

<p>This check will only suggest replacements which yield the same rules as the
existing three-letter ID for at least part of the year (e.g. it will suggest
“America/Chicago” and “Etc/GMT+6” but not “Asia/Shanghai” as a replacement for
“CST”).</p>

<p>Certain 3-letter time zone IDs are not flagged by this check, specifically if
the ID appears in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ZoneId.getAvailableZoneIds()</code>, e.g. “UTC”, “GMT”, “PRC”.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ThreeLetterTimeZoneID")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ThrowableEqualsHashCode<br>
            <small>Overriding Throwable.equals() or hashCode() is discouraged.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Throwables should not override <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">hashCode()</code>.</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Exceptions are Events, Not Value Objects</strong> Philosophically, an exception
represents a unique historical event: something went wrong at a specific
time, in a specific thread, at a specific line of code. It is not a data
container or a value type (like a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">String</code> or a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Money</code> object). Even if two
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">IllegalArgumentException</code>s are thrown with the exact same message (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">"ID
cannot be null"</code>), and perhaps even identical stack traces, they represent
two distinct failures that happened independently. Treating them as “equal”
conceptually conflates two different events.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>The Stack Trace Problem</strong> When an exception is instantiated (or thrown),
Java populates its stack trace via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">fillInStackTrace()</code>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Complexity: Are you going to include the stack trace in your <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code>
comparison? If you do, comparing arrays of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">StackTraceElement</code> is
computationally expensive. Exceptions can also have causes and
suppressed exceptions. This adds expense, too. Also, will all the
transitive causes and suppressed exceptions themselves implement
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code> the way you want? Plus, causes and suppressed exceptions make
exceptions mutable, and mutable objects generally shouldn’t implement
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals()</code>.</li>
      <li>Brittleness: If you don’t include the stack trace, you are saying that
an exception thrown in <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ServiceA</code> is equal to an exception thrown in
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ServiceB</code> just because they share a message or an error code. This
masks critical debugging context.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>It Hides Bad Architecture</strong> The primary reason you would need to override
these methods is if you are placing Exceptions into a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">HashSet</code>, or using
them as keys in a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">HashMap</code>. If you are doing this, you are likely using
Exceptions for normal business logic or control flow, which is a known
anti-pattern. Exceptions are for exceptional circumstances; they are heavy
(because of the stack trace) and slow to generate.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Java Still Sometimes Compares Exceptions by Object Identity</strong> Even if two
exceptions are “the same” according to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">equals</code>, Java will still print both
if it encounters them during a call to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">printStackTrace</code>, and it will allow
one to be a suppressed exception of the other. In both ways, two exceptions
that are “the same” will continue to be treated as different by Java.</p>
  </li>
</ol>

<h3 id="recommended-alternative-a-separate-value-object"><strong>Recommended Alternative: A separate value object</strong></h3>

<p>If you find yourself needing to compare exceptions, <strong>extract the state into a
separate value object.</strong></p>

<p>Instead of this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">UserNotFoundException</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">RuntimeException</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">userId</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">groupId</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="c1">// Override equals and hashCode based on userId and groupId...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Do this: Create a custom Exception that <em>contains</em> a value object (like a Record
or a POJO), and compare the value objects instead.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">UserNotFoundException</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">RuntimeException</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ErrorDetails</span> <span class="n">details</span><span class="o">;</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nf">UserNotFoundException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">ErrorDetails</span> <span class="n">details</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="kd">super</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"%s is not a member of %s:"</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">formatted</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">details</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">userId</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="n">details</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">groupId</span><span class="o">()));</span>
    <span class="k">this</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">details</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">details</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>

  <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">ErrorDetails</span> <span class="nf">getDetails</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">details</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="c1">// Compare the details, not the exceptions!</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e1</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getDetails</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e2</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getDetails</span><span class="o">()))</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ThrowableEqualsHashCode")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            TimeUnitConversionChecker<br>
            <small>This TimeUnit conversion looks buggy: converting from a smaller unit to a larger unit (and passing a constant), converting to/from the same TimeUnit, or converting TimeUnits where the result is statically known to be 0 or 1 are all buggy patterns.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">

          </dl>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This checker flags potential problems with TimeUnit conversions: 1) conversions that are statically known to be equal to 0 or 1; 2) conversions that are converting from a given unit back to the same unit; 3) conversions that are converting from a smaller unit to a larger unit and passing a constant value</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TimeUnitConversionChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ToStringReturnsNull<br>
            <small>An implementation of Object.toString() should never return null.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>

          <h1>
            TraditionalSwitchExpression<br>
            <small>Prefer -> switches for switch expressions</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The newer arrow (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">-&gt;</code>) syntax for switches is preferred to the older colon (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">:</code>)
syntax. The main reason for continuing to use the colon syntax in switch
<em>statements</em> is that it allows fall-through from one statement group to the
next. But in a switch <em>expression</em>, fall-through would only be useful if the
code that falls through has side effects. Burying side effects inside a switch
expression makes code hard to understand.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TraditionalSwitchExpression")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            TruthAssertExpected<br>
            <small>The actual and expected values appear to be swapped, which results in poor assertion failure messages. The actual value should come first.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>Style</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Arguments to a fluent <a href="https://truth.dev">Truth</a> assertion appear to be reversed based on
the argument names.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="kt">int</span> <span class="n">expected</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expected</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">isEqualTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">codeUnderTest</span><span class="o">());</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This is problematic as the quality of Truth’s error message depends on the
argument order. If <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">codeUnderTest()</code> returns <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">2</code>, this code will output:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>expected: 2
but was : 1
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Which will likely make debugging the problem harder. Truth assertions should
follow the opposite order to JUnit assertions. Compare:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">actual</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">isEqualTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expected</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">assertEquals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expected</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">actual</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>See https://truth.dev/faq#order for more details.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TruthAssertExpected")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            TruthConstantAsserts<br>
            <small>Truth Library assert is called on a constant.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The arguments to assertThat method is a constant. It should be a variable or a
method invocation. For eg. switch assertThat(1).isEqualTo(methodCall()) to
assertThat(methodCall()).isEqualTo(1).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TruthConstantAsserts")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            TruthGetOrDefault<br>
            <small>Asserting on getOrDefault is unclear; prefer containsEntry or doesNotContainKey</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Expectation of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Truth.assertThat(map.getOrDefault(key,
defaultValue)).isEqualTo(expectedValue)</code> is unclear if the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">defaultValue</code> is
same as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">expectedValue</code>. If the test passes, its hard to say if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">map</code> contained
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">key, expectedValue</code> as an entry. Most likely, developer intended to verify that
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">map</code> doesn’t contain <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">'key</code> or perhaps map <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">key</code> isn’t mapped to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">defaultValue</code>.</p>

<p>Additionally, same assertion can be simplified if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">defaultValue</code> and
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">expectedValue</code> are different constants to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Truth.assertThat(map.get(key)).isEqualTo(expectedValue)</code>.</p>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">map</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">key</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">expectedValue</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">key</span><span class="o">)).</span><span class="na">isEqualTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expectedValue</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">doesNotContainKey</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">key</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">containsEntry</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">key</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">expectedValue</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">map</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">key</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">defaultValue</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">expectedValue</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">map</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getOrDefault</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">key</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">defaultValue</span><span class="o">)).</span><span class="na">isEqualTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expectedValue</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TruthGetOrDefault")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>
