    <div class="container">
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            WaitNotInLoop<br>
            <small>Because of spurious wakeups, Object.wait() and Condition.await() must always be called in a loop</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.wait()</code> is supposed to block until either another thread invokes the
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.notify()</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.notifyAll()</code> method, or a specified amount of time
has elapsed. The various <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Condition.await()</code> methods have similar behavior.
However, it is possible for a thread to wake up without either of those
occurring; these are called <em>spurious wakeups</em>.</p>

<p>Because of spurious wakeups, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.wait()</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Condition.await()</code> must always
be called in a loop. The correct fix for this varies depending on what you are
trying to do.</p>

<h2 id="wait-until-a-condition-becomes-true">Wait until a condition becomes true</h2>

<p>The incorrect code for this typically looks like:</p>

<p>Thread 1:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">condition</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="n">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrue</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Thread 2:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">condition</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="n">notify</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If the call to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">wait()</code> unblocks because of a spurious wakeup, then
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrue()</code> will be called even though <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">condition</code> is
still false. Instead of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">if</code>, you should use a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">while</code>:</p>

<p>Thread 1:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">condition</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="n">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrue</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This ensures that you only proceed to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrue()</code> if
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">condition</code> is true. Note that the check of the condition variable must be
inside the synchronized block; otherwise you will have a race condition between
checking and setting the condition variable.</p>

<h2 id="wait-until-an-event-occurs">Wait until an event occurs</h2>

<p>The incorrect code for this typically looks like:</p>

<p>Thread 1:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">doStuffAfterEvent</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Thread 2:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="c1">// when event occurs</span>
<span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">notify</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>If the call to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">wait()</code> unblocks because of a spurious wakeup, then
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doStuffAfterEvent()</code> will be called even though the event has not yet occurred.
You should rewrite this code so that the occurrence of the event sets a
condition variable as well as calls <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">notify()</code>, and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">wait()</code> is wrapped in a
while loop checking the condition variable. That is, it should look just like
<a href="#wait_until_a_condition_becomes_true">the previous example</a>.</p>

<h2 id="wait-until-either-a-condition-becomes-true-or-a-timeout-occurs">Wait until either a condition becomes true or a timeout occurs</h2>

<p>The incorrect code for this typically looks like:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">condition</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">timeout</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="n">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrueOrTimeoutHasOccurred</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>A spurious wakeup could cause this to proceed to
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrueOrTimeoutHasOccurred()</code> even if the condition is
still false and time less than the timeout has elapsed. Instead, you should
write:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">now</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">currentTimeMillis</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="kt">long</span> <span class="n">deadline</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">now</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="n">timeout</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(!</span><span class="n">condition</span> <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="n">now</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span> <span class="n">deadline</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">deadline</span> <span class="o">-</span> <span class="n">now</span><span class="o">);</span>
    <span class="n">now</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">currentTimeMillis</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="n">doStuffAssumingConditionIsTrueOrTimeoutHasOccurred</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="wait-for-a-fixed-amount-of-time">Wait for a fixed amount of time</h2>

<p>First, a warning: This type of waiting/sleeping is often done when the real
intent is to wait until some operation completes, and then proceed. If that’s
what you’re trying to do, please consider rewriting your code to use one of the
patterns above. Otherwise you are depending on system-specific timing that
<em>will</em> change when you run on different machines.</p>

<p>The incorrect code for this typically looks like:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// Give some time for the foos to bar</span>
  <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>A spurious wakeup could cause this not to wait for a full 1000 ms. Instead, you
should use <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Thread.sleep()</code>, which is not subject to spurious wakeups:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Thread</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">sleep</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1000</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="wait-forever">Wait forever</h2>

<p>The incorrect code for this typically looks like:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// wait forever</span>
  <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>A spurious wakeup could cause this not to wait forever. You should wrap the call
to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">wait()</code> in a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">while (true)</code> loop:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">synchronized</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="k">this</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// wait forever</span>
  <span class="k">while</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">wait</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="more-information">More information</h2>

<p>See Java Concurrency in Practice section 14.2.2, “Waking up too soon,”
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/Object.html#wait-long-">the Javadoc for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Object.wait()</code></a>,
and the “Implementation Considerations” section in
<a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/locks/Condition.html">the Javadoc for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Condition</code></a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("WaitNotInLoop")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            AutoFactoryAtInject<br>
            <small>@AutoFactory and @Inject should not be used in the same type.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>@AutoFactory classes should not be @Inject-ed, inject the generated factory
instead. Classes that are annotated with @AutoFactory are intended to be
constructed by invoking the factory method on the generated factory. Typically
this is because some of the necessary constructor arguments are not part of the
binding graph. Generated @AutoFactory classes are automatically marked @Inject -
prefer to inject that instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AutoFactoryAtInject")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            BanClassLoader<br>
            <small>Using dangerous ClassLoader APIs may deserialize untrusted user input into bytecode, leading to remote code execution vulnerabilities</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The Java class loading APIs can lead to remote code execution vulnerabilities if
not used carefully. Interpreting potentially untrusted input as bytecode can
give an attacker control of the application.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BanClassLoader")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            BanSerializableRead<br>
            <small>Deserializing user input via the `Serializable` API is extremely dangerous</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The Java <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Serializable</code> API is very powerful, and very dangerous. Any
consumption of a serialized object that cannot be explicitly trusted will likely
result in a critical remote code execution bug that will give an attacker
control of the application. (See
<a href="https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Effective_Java/ka2VUBqHiWkC">Effective Java 3rd Edition §85</a>)</p>

<p>Consider using less powerful serialization methods, such as JSON or XML.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BanSerializableRead")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ClassName<br>
            <small>The source file name should match the name of the top-level class it contains</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: TopLevelName</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>While the Java programming language requires that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public</code> top-level classes are
declared in a source file matching their name (e.g.: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo.java</code> for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">public
class Foo {}</code>, it is possible to declare a non-public top-level class in a file
with a different name (e.g.: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Bar.java</code> for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">class Foo {}</code>).</p>

<p>The Google Java Style Guide §2.1 states, “The source file name consists of the
case-sensitive name of the top-level class it contains, plus the .java
extension.”</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>

<p>Since <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings</code> cannot be applied to package declarations, this
warning can be suppressed by annotating any top-level class in the compilation
unit with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ClassName")</code>.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ComparisonContractViolated<br>
            <small>This comparison method violates the contract</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The comparison contract states that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">sgn(compare(x, y)) == -sgn(compare(y, x))</code>.
(An immediate corollary is that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">compare(x, x) == 0</code>.) This comparison
implementation either a) cannot return 0, b) cannot return a negative value but
may return a positive value, or c) cannot return a positive value but may return
a negative value.</p>

<p>The results of violating this contract can include <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TreeSet.contains</code> never
returning true or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collections.sort</code> failing with an IllegalArgumentException
arbitrarily.</p>

<p>In the long term, essentially all Comparators should be rewritten to use the
Java 8 Comparator factory methods, but our automated migration tools will, of
course, only work for correctly implemented Comparators.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ComparisonContractViolated")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            ExtendsAutoValue<br>
            <small>Do not extend an @AutoValue-like classes in non-generated code.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> classes are intended to be closed, with a single implementation
with known semantics. Implementing them by hand is extremely dangerous.</p>

<p>Here are some common cases where we have seen code that extends <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code>
classes and recommendations for what to do instead:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Overriding the getters to return given values.</strong> This should usually be
replaced by creating an instance of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> class with those
values.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Having the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue.Builder</code> class extend the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> class so it
inherits the abstract getters.</strong> This is wrong since the Builder doesn’t
satisfy the contract of its superclass and is better implemented either by
repeating the methods or by having both the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> class and the
Builder implement a common interface with these getters.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>In other cases of extending the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> class and implementing its
abstract methods, it would be more correct to have the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@AutoValue</code> class
and the other class have a common supertype.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ExtendsAutoValue")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            InsecureCryptoUsage<br>
            <small>A standard cryptographic operation is used in a mode that is prone to vulnerabilities</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: InsecureCipherMode</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This checker looks for usages of standard cryptographic algorithms in
configurations that are prone to vulnerabilities. There are currently three
classes of problems that are covered by this checker:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>Creating an instance of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javax.crypto.Cipher</code> using either the default
settings or the notoriously insecure ECB mode. In particular, Java’s default
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Cipher.getInstance(AES)</code> returns a cipher object that operates in ECB mode.
Dynamically constructed transformation strings are also flagged, as they may
conceal an instance of ECB mode. The problem with ECB mode is that
encrypting the same block of plaintext always yields the same block of
ciphertext. Hence, repetitions in the plaintext translate into repetitions
in the ciphertext, which can be readily used to conduct cryptanalysis. The
use of IES-based cipher algorithms also raises an error, as all currently
available implementations use ECB mode under the hood.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>Using the Diffie-Hellmann protocol on prime fields. Most library
implementations of Diffie-Hellman on prime fields have serious issues that
can be exploited by an attacker. Any operation that may involve this
protocol will be flagged by the checker. Implementations of the protocol
based on elliptic curves (ECDH) are secure and should be used instead.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>Using DSA for digital signatures. Some widely used crypto libraries accept
invalid DSA signatures in specific configurations. The checker will flag all
cryptographic operations that may involve DSA.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("InsecureCryptoUsage")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            IterablePathParameter<br>
            <small>Path implements Iterable<Path>; prefer Collection<Path> for clarity</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p><a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/nio/file/Path.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.nio.file.Path</code></a> implements <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable&lt;Path&gt;</code>, and provides an iterator
over the name elements of the path. Declaring a parameter of type
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable&lt;Path&gt;</code> is not recommended, since it allows clients to pass either an
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Path</code>s, or a single <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Path</code>. Using <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Collection&lt;Path&gt;</code> prevents
clients from accidentally passing a single <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Path</code>.</p>

<p>Example:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">printPaths</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Iterable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Path</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">paths</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">for</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Path</span> <span class="n">path</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="n">paths</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>printPaths(Paths.get("/tmp/hello"));
tmp
hello
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>printPaths(ImmutableList.of(Paths.get("/tmp/hello")));
/tmp/hello
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("IterablePathParameter")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            MissingRuntimeRetention<br>
            <small>Scoping and qualifier annotations must have runtime retention.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: InjectScopeOrQualifierAnnotationRetention</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Qualifier and Scope annotations are used by dependency injection frameworks to
adjust their behavior. Not having runtime retention on scoping or qualifier
annotations will cause unexpected behavior in frameworks that use reflection:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">CreditCardProcessor</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">CreditCardProcessor</span><span class="o">(...)</span> <span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nd">@Qualifier</span>
<span class="nd">@interface</span> <span class="nc">ForTests</span>

<span class="nd">@Provides</span>
<span class="nd">@ForTests</span>
<span class="nc">CreditCardProcessor</span> <span class="nf">providesTestProcessor</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">TestCreditCardProcessor</span><span class="o">(...)</span> <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">...</span>

<span class="nd">@Inject</span>
<span class="nc">MyApp</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">CreditCardProcessor</span> <span class="n">processor</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">processor</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">issueCharge</span><span class="o">(...);</span> <span class="c1">// Issues a charge against a fake!</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Since the Qualifier doesn’t have runtime retention, the Guice provider method
doesn’t see the annotation, and will use the TestCreditCardProcessor for the
normal CreditCardProcessor injection point.</p>

<p>NOTE: Even for dependency injection frameworks traditionally considered to be
compile-time dependent, the JSR-330 specification still requires runtime
retention for both <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javaee/6/api/javax/inject/Qualifier.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Qualifier</code></a> and <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javaee/6/api/javax/inject/Scope.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Scope</code></a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("MissingRuntimeRetention")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            NoAllocation<br>
            <small>@NoAllocation was specified on this method, but something was found that would trigger an allocation</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Like many other languages, Java provides automatic memory management. In Java,
this feature incurs an runtime cost, and can also lead to unpredictable
execution pauses. In most cases, this is a reasonable tradeoff, but sometimes
the loss of performance or predictability is unacceptable. Examples include
pause-sensitive user interface handlers, high query rate server response
handlers, or other soft-realtime applications.</p>

<p>In these situations, you can annotate a few carefully written methods with
@NoAllocation. Methods with this annotation will avoid allocations in most
cases, reducing pressure on the garbage collector. Note that allocations may
still occur in methods with @NoAllocation if the compiler or runtime system
inserts them.</p>

<p>To ease the use of exceptions, allocations are allowed if they occur within a
throw statement. But if the throw statement contains a nested class with methods
annotated with @NoAllocation, those methods will be disallowed from allocating.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("NoAllocation")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            StaticOrDefaultInterfaceMethod<br>
            <small>Static and default interface methods are not natively supported on older Android devices. </small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Static and default interface methods are not natively supported on Android
versions earlier than 7.0. Enable this check for compatibility with older
devices. See
<a href="https://developer.android.com/guide/platform/j8-jack.html">Android Java 8 Documentation</a>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>

<p>To declare default or static methods in interfaces, add a
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticOrDefaultInterfaceMethod")</code> annotation to the
enclosing element.</p>


    </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            StaticQualifiedUsingExpression<br>
            <small>A static variable or method should be qualified with a class name, not expression</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            <dt>Tags</dt><dd>FragileCode</dd>
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: static, static-access, StaticAccessedFromInstance</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>To refer to a static member of another class, we typically <em>qualify</em> that member
name by prepending the name of the class it’s in, and a dot:
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TheClass.theMethod()</code>.</p>

<p>But the Java language also permits you to qualify this call using any
<em>expression</em> (typically, a variable) whose static type is the class that
contains the method: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceOfTheClass.theMethod()</code>.</p>

<p>Doing this creates the appearance of an ordinary polymorphic method call, but it
behaves very differently. For example:</p>

<div class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code>public class Main {
  static class TheClass {
    public static int theMethod() {
      return 1;
    }
  }

  static class TheSubclass extends TheClass {
    public static int theMethod() {
      return 2;
    }
  }

  public static void main(String[] args) {
    TheClass instanceOfTheClass = new TheSubclass();
    System.out.println(instanceOfTheClass.theMethod());
  }
}
</code></pre></div></div>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TheSubclass</code> appears to “override” <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">theMethod</code>, so we might expect this code to
print the number <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">2</code>.</p>

<p>The code, however, prints the number <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">1</code>. The runtime type of
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceOfTheClass</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TheSubclass</code>, is ignored; only the static type of the
reference, as seen by <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">javac</code>, matters.</p>

<p>In fact, the instance that <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">instanceOfTheClass</code> points to is <em>entirely</em>
irrelevant. To prove this, set the variable to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">null</code> and run again. The program
will <em>still</em> print <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">1</code>, not throw a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NullPointerException</code>!</p>

<p>Qualifying a static reference in this way creates an unnecessarily confusing
situation. To prevent it, only qualify static method calls using a class name,
never an expression (that is, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TheClass.theMethod()</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">theMethod()</code>, but not
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">anInstanceOfTheClass.theMethod()</code>).</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("StaticQualifiedUsingExpression")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            SystemExitOutsideMain<br>
            <small>Code that contains System.exit() is untestable.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.exit</code> terminates the java process and returns a status code.
Since it is disruptive to shut down the process within library code,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.exit</code> should not be called outside of a main method.</p>

<p>Instead of calling <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">System.exit</code> consider throwing an unchecked exception to
signal failure.</p>

<p>For example, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">args</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">]);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyUncheckedException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMessage</span><span class="o">());</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">exit</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="c1">// In library code</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">doSomethingElse</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">s</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyCheckedException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">MyUncheckedException</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">args</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">args</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">]);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="c1">// In library code</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">s</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">doSomethingElse</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">s</span><span class="o">)</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">MyCheckedException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">err</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">println</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">e</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getMessage</span><span class="o">());</span>
    <span class="nc">System</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">exit</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("SystemExitOutsideMain")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            TestExceptionChecker<br>
            <small>Using @Test(expected=...) is discouraged, since the test will pass if *any* statement in the test method throws the expected exception</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>The use of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Test(expected = FooException.class)</code> is strongly discouraged, since
the test passes if <em>any</em> statement throws an exception of the expected type.</p>

<p>For example, if <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">add(0, "a")</code> throws an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">UnsupportedOperationException</code> below,
the test will pass without even executing <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">remove(0)</code>, much less testing whether
it throws the right kind of exception. Such false negatives are particularly
likely when testing for common unchecked exceptions like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NullPointerException</code>.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Test</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">expected</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">UnsupportedOperationException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">)</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">testRemoveFails</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">AppendOnlyList</span> <span class="n">list</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">AppendOnlyList</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"a"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">remove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To avoid this issue, prefer JUnit’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">assertThrows()</code> API:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kn">import</span> <span class="nn">static</span> <span class="n">org</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">junit</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Assert</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">assertThrows</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">testRemoveFails</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">AppendOnlyList</span> <span class="n">list</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">AppendOnlyList</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">add</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="s">"a"</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">assertThrows</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">UnsupportedOperationException</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">list</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">remove</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">});</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("TestExceptionChecker")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            UseCorrectAssertInTests<br>
            <small>Java assert is used in testing code. For testing purposes, prefer using Truth-based assertions.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>ERROR</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Java assert statements are not run unless explicitly enabled via runtime flags
to the JVM invocation.</p>

<p>If asserts are not enabled, then a test using assert would continue to pass even
if a bug is introduced since these statements will not be executed. To avoid
this, use one of the assertion libraries that are always enabled, such as
JUnit’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">org.junit.Assert</code> or Google’s Truth library. These will also produce
richer contextual failure diagnostics to aid and accelerate debugging.</p>

<p>Don’t do this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">testArray</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">arr</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">getArray</span><span class="o">();</span>

  <span class="k">assert</span> <span class="n">arr</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="k">assert</span> <span class="n">arr</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">length</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">;</span>
  <span class="k">assert</span> <span class="n">arr</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">].</span><span class="na">equals</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Do this instead:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kn">import</span> <span class="nn">static</span> <span class="n">com</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">google</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">common</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">truth</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Truth</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">assertThat</span><span class="o">;</span>

<span class="nd">@Test</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">testArray</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">arr</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">getArray</span><span class="o">();</span>

  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">arr</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">isNotNull</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">arr</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">hasLength</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="n">assertThat</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">arr</span><span class="o">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="o">]).</span><span class="na">isEqualTo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"hello"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("UseCorrectAssertInTests")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            AnnotationPosition<br>
            <small>Annotations should be positioned after Javadocs, but before modifiers.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Per the <a href="https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s4.8.5.1-type-use-annotation-style">style guide</a>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TYPE_USE</code> annotations should appear
immediately before the type being annotated, and after any modifiers:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">K</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">V</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nd">@Nullable</span> <span class="no">V</span> <span class="nf">getOrNull</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="no">K</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="no">V</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">map</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nd">@Nullable</span> <span class="no">K</span> <span class="n">key</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">map</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">get</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">key</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Non-<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">TYPE_USE</code> annotations should appear before modifiers, as they annotate the
entire element (method, variable, class):</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@VisibleForTesting</span>
<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">reset</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Javadoc must appear before any annotations, or the compiler will fail to
recognise it as Javadoc:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nd">@Nullable</span>
<span class="cm">/** Might return a frobnicator. */</span>
<span class="nc">Frobnicator</span> <span class="nf">getFrobnicator</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AnnotationPosition")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            AssertFalse<br>
            <small>Assertions may be disabled at runtime and do not guarantee that execution will halt here; consider throwing an exception instead</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Java assertions do not necessarily execute at runtime; they may be enabled and
disabled depending on which options are passed to the JVM invocation. An assert
false statement may be intended to ensure that the program never proceeds beyond
that statement. If the correct execution of the program depends on that being
the case, consider throwing an exception instead, so that execution is halted
regardless of runtime configuration.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AssertFalse")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            AssistedInjectAndInjectOnConstructors<br>
            <small>@AssistedInject and @Inject should not be used on different constructors in the same class.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Mixing @Inject and @AssistedInject leads to confusing code and the documentation
specifies not to do it. See
https://google.github.io/guice/api-docs/latest/javadoc/com/google/inject/assistedinject/AssistedInject.html</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AssistedInjectAndInjectOnConstructors")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            AvoidObjectArrays<br>
            <small>Object arrays are inferior to collections in almost every way. Prefer immutable collections (e.g., ImmutableSet, ImmutableList, etc.) over an object array whenever possible.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Object arrays are inferior to collections in almost every way. Prefer <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Set</code>,
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">List</code>, or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Multiset</code> over an object array whenever possible.</p>

<p>A few of these issues are covered, in much greater detail, in
<a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=BIpDDwAAQBAJ">Effective Java Item 28: Prefer lists to arrays</a>.</p>

<h1 id="method-parameters">Method Parameters</h1>

<p>Don’t use object arrays as method parameters:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">createUsers</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">User</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="n">users</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Use an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Iterable</code> instead:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">createUsers</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Iterable</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">User</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="n">users</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h1 id="return-values">Return Values</h1>

<p>Don’t use object arrays as method return values:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">User</span><span class="o">[]</span> <span class="nf">loadUsers</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Use an <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableList</code> (or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableSet</code>) instead:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">ImmutableList</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nc">User</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="nf">loadUsers</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">...</span> <span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h1 id="additional-alternatives">Additional Alternatives</h1>

<p>If you have a 2-dimensional array (e.g., <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Foo[][]</code>), consider using an
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">ImmutableTable&lt;Integer, Integer, Foo&gt;</code> instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("AvoidObjectArrays")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            BindingToUnqualifiedCommonType<br>
            <small>This code declares a binding for a common value type without a Qualifier annotation.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Guice bindings are keyed by a pair of (optional Annotation, Type).</p>

<p>In most circumstances, one doesn’t need the annotation, as there’s really just
one active implementation:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">bind</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">CoffeeMaker</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">to</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">RealCoffeeMaker</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">Office</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">CoffeeMaker</span> <span class="n">coffeeMaker</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>However, in other circumstances, you want to bind a simple value (an integer,
String, double, etc.). You should use a Qualifier annotation to allow you to get
the <em>right</em> Integer back:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">bindConstant</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">annotatedWith</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">HttpPort</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">to</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">80</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">MyWebServer</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nd">@HttpPort</span> <span class="nc">Integer</span> <span class="n">httpPort</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>NOTE: Make sure that your annotation has the <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javaee/6/api/javax/inject/Qualifier.html"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Qualifier</code></a> meta-annotation on
it, otherwise injection systems can’t see them. Guice users can optionally use
<a href="https://github.com/google/guice/wiki/BindingAnnotations"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@BindingAnnotation</code></a>, but Guice also understands <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@Qualifier</code>.</p>

<p>This works great, but if your integer binding <em>doesn’t</em> include a Qualifier, it
just means that you can ask Guice for “the Integer”, and it will give you a
value back:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">bind</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Integer</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">toInstance</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="mi">80</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="nd">@Inject</span> <span class="nc">MyWebServer</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Integer</span> <span class="n">httpsPort</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>To avoid confusion in these circumstances, please use a Qualifier annotation
when binding simple value types.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BindingToUnqualifiedCommonType")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

          <h1>
            BuilderReturnThis<br>
            <small>Builder instance method does not return 'this'</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>This check identifies instance methods in builder classes, and requires that
they either <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">return this;</code>, or are explicitly annotated with
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code>.</p>

<p>Instance methods in builders typically return <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">this</code>, to allow chaining.
Ignoring this result does not indicate a https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/CheckReturnValue bug. For
example, both of the following are fine:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span> <span class="n">builder</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">();</span>
<span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">setBar</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"bar"</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// return value is deliberately unused</span>
<span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">builder</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">Builder</span> <span class="n">builder</span> <span class="o">=</span>
    <span class="nc">Foo</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">builder</span><span class="o">().</span><span class="na">setBar</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"bar"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">build</span><span class="o">();</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Rarely, a builder method may return a new instance, which should not be ignored.
This check requires these methods to be annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code>:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">class</span> <span class="nc">Builder</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nd">@CheckReturnValue</span>
  <span class="nc">Builder</span> <span class="nf">setFoo</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">foo</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">Builder</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">foo</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// returns a new builder instead of this!</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>This check allows the https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/CheckReturnValue enforcement to assume the
return value of instance methods in builders can safely be ignored, unless the
method is explicitly annotated with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@CheckReturnValue</code>.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("BuilderReturnThis")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

          <h1>
            CannotMockFinalClass<br>
            <small>Mockito cannot mock final classes</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Mockito cannot mock final classes. See https://github.com/mockito/mockito/wiki/FAQ
for details.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CannotMockFinalClass")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            CannotMockMethod<br>
            <small>Mockito cannot mock final or static methods, and can't detect this at runtime</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<p><em>Alternate names: MockitoBadFinalMethod, CannotMockFinalMethod</em></p>

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Mockito cannot mock <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> or <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">static</code> methods, and cannot tell at runtime that
this is attempted and fail with an error (as mocking <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">final</code> classes does).</p>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">when(mock.finalMethod())</code> will invoke the real implementation of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">finalMethod</code>.
In some cases, this may wind up accidentally doing what’s intended:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="n">when</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">converter</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">convert</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="o">)).</span><span class="na">thenReturn</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">b</span><span class="o">);</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">convert</code> is final, but under the hood, calls <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">doForward</code>, so we wind up mocking
that method instead.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CannotMockMethod")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

            CatchingUnchecked<br>

          </h1>
        </div>

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            CheckedExceptionNotThrown<br>
            <small>This method cannot throw a checked exception that it claims to. This may cause consumers of the API to incorrectly attempt to handle, or propagate, this exception.</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Java allows methods to declare that they throw checked exceptions even when they
don’t. This can lead to call sites being forced to explicitly handle or
propagate exceptions which provably can never occur. It may also lead readers of
the code to search for possibly throwing paths where none exist.</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">void</span> <span class="nf">validateRequest</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Request</span> <span class="n">request</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="kd">throws</span> <span class="nc">IOException</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="n">checkArgument</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">hasFoo</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="s">"foo must be specified"</span><span class="o">);</span>
<span class="o">}</span>

<span class="nc">Response</span> <span class="nf">handle</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Request</span> <span class="n">request</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="n">validateRequest</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="o">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">IOException</span> <span class="n">e</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="c1">// Required, but unreachable.</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nf">failedResponse</span><span class="o">();</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
  <span class="c1">// ...</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>Including unthrown exceptions can be reasonable where the method is overridable,
as overriding methods will not be able to declare that they throw any exceptions
not included.</p>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("CheckedExceptionNotThrown")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>

    </div>

    <div class="container">

        <div class="col-lg-10 col-md-10">
          <h1>
            ConstantPatternCompile<br>
            <small>Variables initialized with Pattern#compile calls on constants can be constants</small>
          </h1>
        </div>
        <div class="col-lg-1 col-md-2">
          <dl>
            <dt>Severity</dt><dd>WARNING</dd>
            
          </dl>
        </div>
      </div>
      <!--
*** AUTO-GENERATED, DO NOT MODIFY ***
To make changes, edit the @BugPattern annotation or the explanation in docs/bugpattern.
-->

<h2 id="the-problem">The problem</h2>
<p>Method bodies should generally not call
<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">java.util.regex.Pattern#compile(String)</code> with constant arguments. Instead,
define a constant to store that Pattern. This can avoid recompilation of the
regex every time the method is invoked.</p>

<p>That is, prefer this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">Pattern</span> <span class="no">REGEX_PATTERN</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Pattern</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"a+"</span><span class="o">);</span>

<span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">input</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">Matcher</span> <span class="n">matcher</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="no">REGEX_PATTERN</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">matcher</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">input</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">matcher</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">matches</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<p>to this:</p>

<div class="language-java highlighter-rouge"><div class="highlight"><pre class="highlight"><code><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="kt">boolean</span> <span class="nf">doSomething</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">input</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span>
  <span class="nc">Matcher</span> <span class="n">matcher</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Pattern</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">compile</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="s">"a+"</span><span class="o">).</span><span class="na">matcher</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">input</span><span class="o">);</span>
  <span class="k">if</span> <span class="o">(</span><span class="n">matcher</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">matches</span><span class="o">())</span> <span class="o">{</span>
    <span class="o">...</span>
  <span class="o">}</span>
<span class="o">}</span>
</code></pre></div></div>

<h2 id="suppression">Suppression</h2>
<p>Suppress false positives by adding the suppression annotation <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">@SuppressWarnings("ConstantPatternCompile")</code> to the enclosing element.</p>
